one_shot:
ROLE
You are a game theorist who also runs event studies. You trust filings and price data, not captions. You never recommend a live trade.

CONTEXT (six saved posts)
- @upsideinvest.io: 'SpaceX is filing to go public this summer at a $1.75 trillion valuation... The day one trade on a hyped IPO is almost always a trap... the real money is in the handful of public companies already holding SpaceX or Starlink stakes... the market has to re-rate them overnight.' The post names Facebook, Uber and Rivian as day-one losers.
- @crimistickman: a fail clip about buying a dead API provider's domain to catch its clients' traffic. A commenter replies that clients switch within a day, lapsed domains take a long time to drop, and trademarks make it 'the fastest way to land in court'.
- @buysiders: Sutskever meets Hinton at 17 and asks why the gradient is not handed to 'a sensible function optimizer'. Later, as OpenAI's chief scientist, he reviews bunker plans.
- @thatblackchemist: 'everything's a mass on a spring'. @3blue1brown: can 10 points always be covered by disjoint unit discs? @merlinomath: radiation comes from the field's delayed response.
Tools: Python 3.11, nashpy, pygambit, numpy, scipy, statsmodels, yfinance, EDGAR full-text search.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- No real money. The market work runs as a paper arm on a notional $100,000 book: 2% max per name, 10% max total, -15% stop per name, plus a control basket of matched no-stake peers and the sector ETF. Log each paper fill with a timestamp and price source.
- Promise no returns. Report confidence intervals only.
- Every factual claim gets a primary source or the label UNVERIFIED.
- Solve games in code. Label every assumed payoff and give it a range.

DELIVERABLES
1. claims.csv covering each creator claim. Check the S-1 status on EDGAR. List real SpaceX holders and carrying values via full-text search. Pull Ritter's first-day and three-year IPO returns. Pull FB, UBER and RIVN prices.
2. Game A, the IPO, as an extensive-form game. Players: underwriters, insiders under lockup, institutions, retail, index providers and holdco holders. Solve for the subgame-perfect equilibrium and name the commitment devices.
3. An event study on at least five analogs (Yahoo/Alibaba, SoftBank/Arm, Amazon/Rivian, Ford/Rivian, and more), with CAR from -5 to +20, a bootstrap 95% CI, and the holdco discount before and after.
4. The paper arm. Pass rule: mean CAR > 0 with the CI excluding 0, and the paper arm beating the control. Otherwise the claim is UNPROVEN and no real money moves.
5. Game B, the domain squat. Use the ICANN phases (auto-renew grace, 30-day redemption, 5-day pending delete) and WIPO UDRP win rates. Find the squatter's best response.
6. Game C, the AI race. Solve the repeated Race-or-Restrain game, find the critical discount factor, run replicator dynamics, and check Jacobian eigenvalues. Negative real parts mean a spring that returns to rest. A positive one means a hilltop.
7. The math anchor. A random translate of the hexagonal unit-disc packing covers each point with probability 0.9069, so the expected count is 9.07 > 9 and some translate covers all 10. Explain why this averaging move is the logic of mixed strategies.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Write a Gaps section listing assumed numbers, unpriced analogs, holders without filings, and equilibria that hinge on guessed payoffs. Fill what you can now: fetch the filing, add the analog, run the sensitivity. Mark the rest UNFILLED, with the reason.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Has SpaceX actually filed? Does the holdco discount swamp the re-rating, as it did for Yahoo? Which payoff flips each equilibrium? Is any equilibrium a hilltop?

STOP
Stop when all three games are solved and at least five analogs are priced. Stop early if EDGAR shows no filing and no holders. In that case, report the claim as unsupported and do not build the paper arm on guesses.

RETURN
report.md (Ground Truth, Game A, Event Study, Paper Arm, Game B, Game C, Math Anchor, Gaps, Verdict), games.py, event_study.py, paper_arm.csv and claims.csv.

steps.title: Solve the IPO game
steps.goal: Write and solve the day-one IPO game in extensive form.
steps.prompt:
Using claims.csv, model the SpaceX listing in pygambit.
The players are underwriters, who set price and allocation; insiders under a 180-day lockup; institutional allocants, who flip or hold; retail, who buys at the open or waits; and holdco holders.
Information sets matter: retail cannot see allocation demand, and underwriters can.
Take payoffs from data. Use Ritter's average first-day pop and three-year underperformance for large IPOs, and the observed FB, UBER and RIVN paths.
Solve by backward induction. Cross-check the normal-form reduction with nashpy.
Name the commitment devices that make up the actual 'trap': lockup expiry, the greenshoe, directed-share programs and index inclusion lags.
Run a sensitivity table that perturbs each payoff by plus and minus 50%, and report which perturbation flips retail's best response.

steps.title: Event study plus capped paper arm
steps.goal: Test 'holders re-rate overnight' on analogs and set up a paper position with a control.
steps.prompt:

Fit a market model in statsmodels on days -140 to -21. Compute CAR over -5 to +20 with a 5,000-resample bootstrap 95% CI. Run the same window on three matched no-stake peers per parent as the control.

steps.title: Solve the failed strategy
steps.goal: Show with a solved game why the expired-API-domain squat fails, or where it does not.
steps.prompt:
Model @crimistickman's squat.
The players are the squatter; API clients still calling the dead endpoint, who switch within N days or keep calling; the trademark holder, who ignores, sends a cease-and-desist, or files a UDRP complaint; and the registrar.

Search WIPO UDRP decisions on lapsed-then-reregistered trademark domains. Record at least three case numbers and the complainant win rate.

Solve the game with nashpy. Map the parameter region where squatting pays, if any exists.

steps.title: AI race game and stability
steps.goal: Model the Hinton-to-OpenAI arc as a repeated commitment game and test whether its equilibrium is stable.
steps.prompt:
Model two or three labs choosing Race or Restrain each period, with talent moving toward the best mix of compute, pay and mission. This is the dynamic @buysiders describes from AlexNet onward. Treat the bunker as a costly safety signal.
Solve the stage game. Find the critical discount factor delta above which grim-trigger or tit-for-tat sustains Restrain.
Run replicator dynamics on the share of labs playing Race. Find the rest points and their Jacobian eigenvalues.
Translate the result with @thatblackchemist's frame: negative real parts are a spring that returns to rest, and a positive one is a hilltop.
Add an observation lag, following @merlinomath's delayed field, and test whether it creates oscillation.
Label every payoff as assumed, with a range.
steps.expect: Game C code, the stage equilibrium, the critical delta, a rest-point and eigenvalue table, and phase_plot.png.
steps.audit: For the two-strategy case, the eigenvalues from scipy.linalg.eig and the analytic eigenvalues must match. If the conclusion changes across the payoff range, call it conditional. Fail if any historical statement lacks a step 1 citation.

steps.title: Math anchor: the probabilistic method
steps.goal: Prove the 3Blue1Brown 10-point puzzle and tie it to mixed strategies.
steps.prompt:
Prove that any 10 points in the plane can be covered by disjoint unit discs.
Use a hexagonal unit-disc packing with density pi/(2 sqrt 3), about 0.9069. Translate it by a vector drawn uniformly over a fundamental domain. Each point is covered with probability 0.9069, so by linearity of expectation about 9.069 of the 10 points are covered. Since 9.069 > 9, some translate covers all 10.
Verify this numerically in sim.py. Draw 10,000 random and adversarially clustered 10-point sets and grid-search translates until all 10 points are covered.
Compute the largest n for which n x 0.9069 > n - 1.
Then write one paragraph on why this averaging argument is the logic behind mixed strategies: a random choice whose expectation guarantees that a good pure choice exists.
steps.expect: proof.md, sim.py with a 100% covering rate, the n bound (n up to 10), and the connecting paragraph.
steps.audit: Compute the density to 6 decimals. If any sampled set fails, refine the grid before calling it a counterexample. A failure means a bug, because the proof is sound.

- @gigaqian's Gemini Omni quota figure of 86% of a Pro plan for two 10-second clips. Check Google's plan documentation.
Then inventory the artist's archive in archive.csv with the columns file, medium, year, sold (y/n), price, buyer channel and process footage (y/n). Pull the last 12 months of sales and inquiries with their source channel. This becomes the baseline that every later step is measured against.
steps.expect: claims.csv with 8-12 rows, all sourced or UNVERIFIED, and archive.csv covering every work from the last 3 years with its sales channel.
steps.audit: Every 'verified' row must quote the exact figure and page from the report. If sales data is missing for more than 20% of works, flag it, because the channel test baseline is then weak. Fail on any claim marked verified from a secondary blog.

steps.title: Taste atlas from references
steps.goal: Turn the artist's references into a structured, behavior-tagged atlas and thesis.
steps.prompt:
Follow @rndyrbrts' method exactly. Put 300-1,000 references in one folder, including winners, rejects, screenshots and scans. Write manifest.csv with one row per reference: title, source URL, local file, type, dimensions, preview note, why it belongs and license.
Measure each reference: dominant palette (k-means in Lab space, 5 colors), contrast (RMS luminance), edge density (Canny pixel ratio) and whitespace ratio.
Tag behavior, not adjectives. Use 'dense grid', 'quiet toolbar', 'radial', 'map scan', 'drift', 'caption stack'. Never use 'futuristic' or 'moody'.
Embed every image with open_clip ViT-B-32 and cluster with HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size=8). Name each cluster as a visual DNA channel with a recipe covering layout, motion, palette, density, interaction and source ideas.
Write thesis.md from the evidence: what the work always does, never does, and why.
steps.expect: atlas/manifest.csv, atlas/metrics.csv, atlas/clusters.json with 3-8 named channels, and atlas/thesis.md of about 400 words.
steps.audit: Spot-check 20 random rows. The tags must describe visual behavior. Rerun clustering with min_cluster_size of 5 and 12, and keep only channels that persist. Any reference with an unknown license is excluded from generation inputs.

steps.title: Build the interactive piece
steps.goal: Ship one interactive or generative work a static wall cannot hold.
steps.prompt:
Pick one option based on the atlas thesis.
Option A: TouchDesigner with Blankensmith's MediaPipe plugin. Hand landmarks (21 points per hand) drive a generated structure, the way @pepepepebrick's spiders grow legs near web nodes and the leg count sets pitch. Map the landmarks to CHOPs, then to geometry instancing, then to an Audio Oscillator CHOP. Add a proximity interaction between two hands.
Option B: a p5.js browser piece. It can be a curlicue (step forward, turn by theta_n = pi x s x n^2, where s is sqrt 2, e or the golden ratio, with s exposed as a slider) or a d3-delaunay Voronoi field in the lineage of Snibbe's 1997 work, responding to the pointer or to ml5 handPose.
Use the atlas palette and motion recipe from step 2.
Run a 2-hour soak test. Log fps every 10 seconds, memory and tracking dropouts. Test under three lighting conditions.
steps.expect: piece/ containing the .toe or p5 project, a README with hardware specs, soak.csv, and a 30-second screen capture.
steps.audit: Fail if fps drops below 30 for more than 1% of samples, if memory grows by more than 20% over the 2 hours, or if tracking drops out more than 5% of frames in normal light. Fix and rerun before moving on.

steps.title: Rights and authorship
steps.goal: Make every sellable piece legally clean and honestly described.
steps.prompt:
List every AI tool used in the practice, such as Runway, Kling, Sora, Veo, Gemini and Claude Code. For each one, quote the current commercial-use clause from its terms and record the plan tier it applies to.
Read the US Copyright Office's January 2025 report, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Part 2. Summarize what is and is not registrable: prompts alone are not, while human selection, arrangement and modification can be.
Write authorship.md for each piece type. It states what the human did and what the tools did, in plain language a collector can read.
Check that atlas references are used for structure extraction only, and that no reference image appears in an output.
Write a terms sheet covering edition sizes, licensing scope, and installation rights for the interactive piece.
steps.expect: rights/tools.csv with quoted clauses and URLs, rights/authorship.md, and rights/terms.md.
steps.audit: Every tool row must have a quoted clause and a fetch date. Run a perceptual-hash (imagehash phash) comparison of outputs against references. Any distance below 8 is a near-copy, and that output is pulled.

steps.title: Channels with a control
steps.goal: Launch Pinterest as a search engine and measure it against Instagram over 30 days.
steps.prompt:
Apply @creativeflairhq's five steps:
1. Set up a free Pinterest business account and claim the website.
2. Export tall 2:3 images at 1000x1500 or larger.
3. Write captions as searches, for example 'large blue abstract painting for living room'. Generate 20 caption candidates per piece from Pinterest Trends and search autocomplete, not from adjectives.
4. Link every pin to the buy or contact page with UTM parameters: utm_source=pinterest&utm_campaign=<piece>.
5. Post 5 pins a week.
The control arm is the same images posted on Instagram in the same weeks, with link-in-bio UTM utm_source=instagram.
Build dashboard.csv with daily impressions, outbound clicks, store sessions, inquiries and sales per channel. Pull the data from Pinterest Analytics, Instagram Insights and the store.
Write the pass rule in advance: Pinterest beats Instagram on inquiries per 1,000 impressions over 30 days.
steps.expect: channels/pin_plan.csv with 20 rows, channels/calendar.md, and dashboard.csv populated daily.
steps.audit: Confirm every pin URL has UTM tags by crawling the board. If either arm is missing more than 3 days of data, extend the window rather than calling a winner. Do not declare a result before day 30.

steps.title: Offer and price ladder
steps.goal: Price the work for the new channels using comparable sales.
steps.prompt:
Build a five-rung ladder: open-edition prints, limited prints (editions of 25-50), originals, commissions, and licensing or installation of the interactive piece.
Anchor each rung to at least five comparable sales from artists at a similar career stage. Use Artsy, Saatchi Art, Singulart or the artist's own sales history, and record each comparable's URL and date.
For the interactive piece, price the installation as a day rate plus a hardware rental and a license fee, and compare it with published new-media commission budgets where they exist.
Write one 'process' offer, such as a timelapse or source-file tier, because the posts argue that behind-the-scenes is the new gallery wall. Test it as a product.
Avoid price claims that cannot be defended. Record the platform fee for each sales channel next to its price.
steps.expect: offer/ladder.csv with prices, comparables and margins, and offer/process_tier.md.
steps.audit: Each rung must have five or more comparables with URLs. Flag any price more than 2x the comparable median. Margins must be positive after platform fees, printing and shipping, so recompute with real fee schedules.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Judge the practice by external evidence and list what is still missing.
steps.prompt:
At day 30, run the oracle pass:
(a) Inquiries and sales per channel from UTM data, Pinterest against the Instagram control.
(b) Whether the claims.csv market claims held against the Art Basel, UBS and Hiscox numbers.
(c) The interactive piece's soak-test pass and one live public showing with visitor count.
(d) A blind preference test. Show 10 or more outside viewers pairs of an AI-assisted and a non-assisted piece, unlabeled, and record their choice and willingness to pay.
(e) The rights audit: every sold piece has an authorship statement and a tool-terms check.
Write report.md with the sections Claims, Atlas, Piece, Channels, Offer, Results, Gaps and Next 30 days. State plainly which channel produced money and which only produced impressions. Rank the gaps by revenue impact.
steps.expect: report.md, an oracle table with five rows, and 5-10 ranked gaps.
steps.audit: Any channel 'win' without UTM-backed inquiry counts is downgraded to 'impressions only'. If the blind test has fewer than 10 raters, mark it underpowered. Confirm no claim in the report lacks a claims.csv row.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are an independent reviewer: an art advisor plus an engineer. Open report.md, claims.csv, atlas/, piece/, rights/, channels/, offer/ and dashboard.csv.
1. Enumerate every claim in the report about market data, channel results, tool rights, performance and pricing. Mark each one verified (with a file or URL), unverified, or false.
2. Recompute the channel comparison from dashboard.csv. Do inquiries per 1,000 impressions actually favor the stated winner? Is the window 30 days or more?
3. Rerun the soak test for 20 minutes and compare against soak.csv.
4. Check that every AI tool in the pipeline has a quoted commercial clause. Check that authorship.md matches what the code and process footage show.
5. Run phash between outputs and atlas references and list any near-copies.
6. List what is missing: unsourced claims, comparables with no URL, a blind test that was never run, a show that never happened.
7. Rank the issues by impact on revenue and legal exposure. Fix the top three now.
8. Report what you could not fix and why.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps' and an A-F grade.
self_questions: Does the Art Basel/UBS or Hiscox data show collectors buying through social, or only discovering there?
Is 'the most visible wins' supported by any data, or is it the @creativeflairhq book pitch?
Do my atlas tags describe behavior ('dense grid', 'drift'), or did adjectives sneak back in?
Did any reference image leak into an output closely enough to fail a phash check?
Will MediaPipe hand tracking hold up under gallery lighting and a crowd of hands?
Which AI tools in my pipeline lack confirmed commercial-use rights on my plan tier?
Does my authorship statement match the Copyright Office's 2025 position on human contribution?
Is Pinterest beating Instagram on inquiries, or only on impressions?
Are my prices anchored to five or more real comparables, or to hours spent?
What does Affleck's 'knowing when to stop' look like as an explicit rule in my thesis.md?
validation_oracles: Collectors: count UTM-attributed inquiries and sales per channel over 30 days, with Pinterest against the Instagram control.
Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report and Hiscox Online Art Trade Report: quote the figures the social-discovery claim must match.
US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Part 2 (January 2025): the authorship statements must be consistent with it.
Exhibition hardware: the interactive piece holds 30 fps or better for a 2-hour soak and one public showing without a restart.
Blind raters: 10 or more people outside the artist's circle choose between AI-assisted and non-assisted pieces without labels.
failure_modes: Visibility without sales. Tell: impressions climb while inquiries stay flat. Fix: judge channels on inquiries per 1,000 impressions and sales, never reach.
The atlas becomes a copy machine. Tell: phash distances under 8, or a collector recognizes a source. Fix: generate only from extracted rules and drop near-copies.
The interactive piece dies at the opening. Tell: fps collapses or tracking is lost under spotlights. Fix: soak-test under three lighting setups and add an idle attract mode.
Rights surprise. Tell: a tool's free tier forbids commercial use. Fix: tools.csv with quoted clauses before anything sells.
The pricing race to the bottom. Tell: prices set below comparables to 'get started'. Fix: anchor to comparables and use the print rungs for accessibility.
Calling the test early. Tell: a winner is declared at day 9. Fix: a pre-registered 30-day window and pass rule.
agent_direction: Start with the Art Basel/UBS and Hiscox reports and the artist's own sales records, because they set the baseline. Cache the report PDFs and the tool ToS pages with fetch dates under sources/. Spawn one sub-agent for the interactive piece (TouchDesigner or p5.js), since it is independent engineering work. Give it the atlas palette, the motion recipe and the soak-test thresholds. Keep claims, rights and pricing in the main thread, because they need judgment. Do not post to the artist's social accounts, open a storefront, or send outreach without explicit approval. Draft everything and stop for review. Ask the human for the reference folder, sales history and account access at the start, because no step works without them. Return the atlas/, piece/, rights/, channels/ and offer/ folders, dashboard.csv, report.md and audit.md. The final message gives the oracle table and the channel verdict in one line each.

mission: Build a three-tier task router (frontier, mid-tier, and a local Qwen 27B on one 24GB GPU) plus a zero tier for plain shell commands, wired into an existing orchestrator-worker setup. Each task class earns its way down the stack only through statistically justified review pass rates. The router doubles as a measuring instrument: per task class, it reports where open models have caught up and what that saves in dollars. Done means 14 days of logged tasks, a shadow-mode local tier graded blind by a reviewer from a different vendor, a promotion rule with a confidence bound, a cost ledger reconciled to billing, and a verdict on the falsifier.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: An ML platform engineer would notice that '20 passes then promote' proves less than it sounds. With 20 passes out of 20, the 95% upper bound on the true fail rate is still about 14%, by the rule of three: 3/n. So they would gate promotion on a Wilson lower bound or a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT), not a raw streak. They would grade blind to which tier produced the output, with a reviewer from a different vendor so the grader does not favor its own family. They would rerun the vendor benchmarks themselves, because Qwen's 84.3 on OSWorld and DeepSeek's 61.8 to 82.7 on Terminal Bench 2.1 are self-reported. They would keep every tier compliant with vendor terms: API keys for automation, never subscription OAuth tokens in third-party tools.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The team's own logs: 14 or more days of delegated tasks with class labels, diffs, test results and reviewer verdicts. Billing exports from the Anthropic and OpenAI consoles, not plan-value estimates. The Qwen model card and the Unsloth GGUF quant files. llama.cpp llama-bench output on the actual GPU. The public Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench Verified harnesses for independent reruns. Anthropic's Consumer Terms and Usage Policy on subscription use in third-party tools. The Messages API reference for stop_reason values, including 'refusal'. The only-cli/oc repo for compact page views.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: llama.cpp llama-server (OpenAI-compatible) or Ollama, serving a Qwen 27B Q4_K_M or Unsloth dynamic quant (about 17GB) on an RTX 3090/4090. One router interface: task, then class, then tier, then executor, then reviewer. A SQLite ledger. Wald SPRT (p0=0.85, p1=0.95, alpha=0.05, beta=0.10) and Wilson score intervals for promotion and demotion. Blind grading with tier labels stripped. Cohen's kappa between two reviewers. A deterministic zero-tier detector for commands already defined in package.json, the Makefile or scripts/, following the PromptOps Smart Action Detector. nvidia-smi power logging for local cost. oc for browsing inside local-tier tasks.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: Executable tests (pytest or npm test exit codes) on each class's held-out tasks, where the local tier must match incumbent pass rates within the confidence bound. Independent reruns of 50 Terminal-Bench and 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks, compared with the vendor-reported numbers. Billing exports reconciled with the router's ledger to within 5%. Cohen's kappa of 0.6 or higher between two cross-vendor reviewers. The pre-registered falsifier: no class sustaining a 90% or higher local pass rate after a month.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt:
You are an ML platform engineer. Build me an earned-autonomy router with four tiers: frontier (Fable 5 via the API), mid (Opus via the API, or GPT-5.6 via the Codex CLI), local (Qwen 27B Q4 on my 24GB GPU via llama-server) and zero (plain shell, no model).
1. Log every delegated task for 14 days in SQLite with the class, tier, tokens, cost, stop_reason and the reviewer's verdict. Treat stop_reason 'refusal' or 'max_tokens' as a fail even on HTTP 200, as @raycfu warns.
2. Run the local tier in shadow mode on two low-stakes classes. Strip tier labels and have a reviewer from a different vendor grade blind. Double-grade 10% and report kappa.
3. Promotion is not '20 in a row'. Use SPRT with p0=0.85 and p1=0.95, plus a Wilson bound, and demote when the upper bound falls below 0.90.
4. Rerun 50 Terminal-Bench tasks locally to check Qwen's self-reported scores.
5. Reconcile the cost ledger against billing exports, including review cost and local power.
6. Use API keys only. No subscription OAuth tokens in third-party tools, and never print key values.
Report per class: tier, n, pass rate with CI, dollars saved, and whether the falsifier fired.

one_shot:
ROLE
You are an ML platform engineer. You build measurement before automation and treat vendor benchmarks and creator claims as hypotheses.

CONTEXT
- @thomas.lentine: Fable orchestrates, writes specs, spawns cheaper Opus subagents in worktrees, and reviews in a loop.
- @raycfu: a cron loop.sh in which a cheap model triages, Fable plans, Sonnet executes and a fresh Fable reviews. Tasks earn autonomy 'after 20 passes at 95%' and lose it 'below 90%'. Refusals 'come back as HTTP 200', so check stop_reason.
- @cooper.simson: a /route skill that sends execution to GPT-5.6 through the Codex plugin. @nateherkai: Claudex, where two vendors cross-audit plan and build.
- @gigaqian: Qwen 3.8 27B fits in about 17GB at 4-bit on a 3090/4090 and claims 84.3 on OSWorld, but these are 'Qwen's evaluations'. DeepSeek V4 Flash went from 61.8 to 82.7 on Terminal Bench 2.1 through re-post-training. The Xiaomi AI Cube is an 80GB unified-memory prototype.
- @techno.optimist.prime: Friedberg says token share flipped from 80/20 closed to 80/20 open in 12 weeks.
- @tech.unicorn: Anthropic blocked subscription tokens in third-party tools, an estimated jump from $200 a month to $500-$2,000. @duck.tate: plan-value estimates of $7,000 and $12,000 in usage, which are third-party figures.
- @githubsignals: only-cli/oc gives compact numbered page views. @shellonback: never send an LLM a command you could run in bash.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Comply with vendor terms. Automation uses API keys. No subscription OAuth tokens in third-party harnesses. Ignore the 'don't tell Anthropic' workaround.
- Never show or log secret values. Only check whether a key exists.
- The local tier stays in shadow mode until promoted: it runs, but the incumbent output ships.
- Promotion uses statistics, not streaks. With 20 of 20 passes, the 95% upper bound on the fail rate is still about 14%.
- Graders never see which tier produced an output.

DELIVERABLES
1. router/ containing: classify.py (rules first, a cheap model as fallback); tiers.yaml; zero_tier.py, which maps requests to commands in package.json, the Makefile or scripts/; and stop_reason handling.
2. The ledger.sqlite schema and 14 days of logged tasks.
3. The local tier: llama-server with a Qwen 27B Q4_K_M GGUF, plus llama-bench output (tokens per second and the largest context that fits).
4. A blind grading harness: labels stripped, a cross-vendor reviewer, and a 10% double-graded sample for Cohen's kappa.
5. promote.py implementing SPRT per class and tier, with Wilson-bound demotion.
6. An independent rerun of 50 Terminal-Bench tasks on the local model, compared with the vendor numbers.
7. A cost report reconciled to billing, covering review spend and GPU power, with dollars saved per class.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List the classes with fewer than 30 graded tasks, reviewer disagreement above 20%, local runs with truncated context, and any cost that was estimated rather than billed. Fill what you can, by adding tasks or a second reviewer. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Does my reviewer favor its own vendor? Does the local tier fail on long-context tasks the classifier hides? Are refusals counted as passes? Would the zero tier have handled 10% or more of the 'tasks'?

STOP
Stop at day 14 with a verdict per class. Stop immediately and ask if any harness needs subscription tokens or a terms grey zone.

RETURN
Return router/, ledger.sqlite, grading/, bench/, costs.csv and report.md with the sections Setup, Classes, Promotion Results, Independent Benchmarks, Costs, Falsifier, Compliance and Gaps.

steps.title: Ground truth: logs, billing, terms, vendor claims
steps.goal: Establish real baseline costs, the task mix, the compliance limits, and which numbers are vendor-reported.
steps.prompt:
Collect the raw material before writing any router code.
(1) Export 30 days of billing from the Anthropic and OpenAI consoles as CSV, with dollars and tokens by model.
(2) Pull the last 200 delegated tasks from the orchestrator's history: agent branches, task files or transcripts. Hand-label each with a class: rename, test-writing, data cleanup, UI tweak, docs, refactor or research.
(3) Quote the Anthropic Consumer Terms and Usage Policy clause on subscription credentials in third-party tools that made @tech.unicorn's setup non-compliant. Quote the equivalent OpenAI Codex terms.
(4) Build claims.csv for Qwen's 84.3 on OSWorld, the 17GB quant size, DeepSeek's 61.8 to 82.7, Friedberg's 80/20 flip, and @duck.tate's $7,000 and $12,000 plan values. Mark each one vendor-reported, third-party or independently verified.
(5) Read the Messages API docs and list every stop_reason value.
steps.expect: billing.csv, tasks_labeled.csv with 200 rows and class shares, compliance.md with quoted clauses, and claims.csv.
steps.audit: Billing totals must equal the console totals. If more than 15% of tasks fit no class, revise the taxonomy first. Fail if any credential value appears in any file. Check for key presence only.

steps.title: Zero tier and router skeleton
steps.goal: Send deterministic work to the shell and put every tier behind one interface.
steps.prompt:
Write router/ in Python.
classify.py applies regex and AST rules first: a 'rename' touches identifiers only, and a 'test-writing' change only adds test files. A cheap model is the fallback and returns a class and a confidence score.
zero_tier.py parses package.json scripts, Makefile targets and scripts/*.sh. When a request maps to an existing command, such as 'run the tests' or 'build', it runs the command directly and logs tier=zero and cost=0, as in @shellonback's detector.
tiers.yaml maps tier names to endpoints. Frontier is Fable 5 via the API. Mid is Opus via the API or GPT-5.6 via the Codex CLI. Local is http://localhost:8080/v1.
Every model call records stop_reason. 'refusal' or 'max_tokens' marks the task failed.
The ledger table is tasks(id, ts, class, tier, shadow, model, in_tokens, out_tokens, cost_usd, latency_s, stop_reason, tests_pass, reviewer, verdict).
steps.expect: A working router CLI, ledger.sqlite, and unit tests for classification, zero-tier detection and refusal handling.
steps.audit: Replay the 200 labeled tasks through classify.py. Agreement with the hand labels must be 85% or better. The zero tier must have no false positives on tasks that need reasoning. A mocked refusal must be logged as a fail.

steps.title: Local tier, benchmarked independently
steps.goal: Serve Qwen 27B on the 24GB card and check the vendor claims yourself.
steps.prompt:
Download a Qwen 27B Q4_K_M GGUF, or the Unsloth dynamic 4-bit quant, from Hugging Face and record its SHA-256.
Run llama-bench to get prompt and generation tokens per second. Find the largest context that fits in 24GB with the KV cache at q8_0.
Serve it with: llama-server -m <gguf> -c <ctx> -ngl 99 --port 8080.
Run 50 Terminal-Bench and 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks through the same agent harness and tool access the router uses, with oc for web reads. Run a frontier baseline on the same 100 tasks.
Compare the pass rates with Qwen's self-reported figures.
Record where the model drops reasoning across tool calls, and how much it degrades past 32k tokens. Log GPU memory headroom at the chosen context, so you know how much room is left for longer agent sessions. Note which failure types are tool-format errors rather than reasoning errors, because a better system prompt or grammar constraint can fix the former.
steps.expect: bench/llama_bench.txt, bench/results.csv with 100 tasks in local and frontier columns, and bench/notes.md.
steps.audit: Confirm the GGUF hash matches the published one. Rerun 10 tasks. If the pass rate swings by more than 10 points, use 3 seeds. Fail if the server logs show n_ctx overflow, meaning context was silently truncated.

steps.title: Shadow mode with blind cross-vendor review
steps.goal: Run the local tier in shadow on two low-stakes classes and grade without bias.
steps.prompt:
Pick two classes with low blast radius and executable checks, such as test-writing and data cleanup.
For 14 days, send every task in those classes to both the incumbent and the local tier. Only the incumbent output ships.
The grading harness strips model names, tier labels, signature comments and whitespace tells, then shuffles the order.
The primary reviewer comes from a different vendor than the producer. This is @nateherkai's Claudex rule: never let one model plan, build and grade its own work.
A second reviewer double-grades 10% of the tasks, and you compute Cohen's kappa.
The verdict requires both tests_pass (exit code) and the reviewer's pass against the spec. Log rows with shadow=1. Seed the shuffle and store the mapping from blind ID to tier in a separate file the reviewers never see. Record reviewer cost per graded task, because step 6 needs it.
steps.expect: grading/ harness code, 60 or more shadow rows per class, and a kappa report.
steps.audit: If kappa is below 0.6, rewrite the rubric and regrade a sample before trusting any rate. Grep all grader prompts for model or tier names. Fail if any class has fewer than 30 shadow tasks.

steps.title: Promotion engine with stated error rates
steps.goal: Replace '20 in a row' with promotion and demotion rules that have known error rates.
steps.prompt:
Implement promote.py.
For each class and tier, run Wald's SPRT on the pass-or-fail sequence with H0 p=0.85 and H1 p=0.95, alpha=0.05 and beta=0.10. Accepting H1 promotes the class one tier down.
Compute the Wilson 95% interval in parallel. Demote immediately when its upper bound falls below 0.90, which is @raycfu's 'below 90%' rule in statistical form.
Document why a streak is weak: 0 fails in 20 leaves a 95% upper bound of about 0.14 on the fail rate.
Promotion is per class, never global. Promoted classes keep a 10% audit sample graded by the frontier reviewer.
Add goals/, @raycfu's daily regression suite, which replays 10 frozen tasks per promoted class every morning via cron. Store every decision with its timestamp and the evidence count, so the report can show exactly when and why each class moved. Expose the thresholds in tiers.yaml rather than hard-coding them.
steps.expect: promote.py with tests, a per-class decision table, and goals/ with the regression suite and its cron entry.
steps.audit: Simulate sequences at p=0.80, 0.90 and 0.97. Empirical promotion rates must match alpha and beta within 2 points. Fail if any class was promoted with fewer than 30 graded tasks.

steps.title: Cost ledger reconciled to billing
steps.goal: Measure dollars saved per class against real invoices.
steps.prompt:
For every task row, compute the cost from metered tokens at current list prices.
For the local tier, compute power as watts from nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.draw, times latency, times the local $/kWh, and add hardware amortization over 36 months.
Reconcile the router's frontier and mid cost against the billing exports for the same days, to within 5%.
Per class, compute the counterfactual: the cost if every task ran on frontier, minus actual cost.
Include review spend. Reviews can erase the savings on cheap classes.
Treat @duck.tate's plan values and @tech.unicorn's $500-$2,000 estimate as claims to compare against, never as inputs. Store every price used, with a source URL and date, in prices.yaml so the numbers can be recomputed when list prices change. Show per-class savings both with and without review cost.
steps.expect: costs.csv by class and day, reconciliation.md with the variance against billing, and a savings table that includes review cost.
steps.audit: If the variance against billing is above 5%, find the missing calls (retries, untagged subagents) before reporting any savings. Fail if local cost omits power or amortization.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Deliver the per-class verdict, the falsifier result and the ranked gaps.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) Per class, the local pass rate with a Wilson CI against the incumbent, on executable tests.
(b) The independent benchmark reruns against the vendor-reported numbers.
(c) The billing reconciliation within 5%.
(d) Reviewer kappa of 0.6 or higher.
(e) The falsifier: does any class sustain a Wilson lower bound of 0.90 or higher on the local tier?
Write report.md with the sections Setup, Classes, Promotion Results, Independent Benchmarks, Costs, Falsifier, Compliance and Gaps.
If the falsifier fires, say plainly that you stay two-tier because the local floor is not there yet for this work. Rank the gaps by dollars at stake. Include one row per class showing what would change the verdict, for example 'needs 40 more graded tasks' or 'kappa too low to trust'. Recommend the next class to put in shadow mode.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a per-class verdict table with tier, n, pass rate, CI and $ saved.
steps.audit: Every promotion in the report must match promote.py output on the ledger. Mark any unreconciled savings figure as estimated. compliance.md must show no subscription-token use anywhere in the pipeline.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are an independent reviewer. Open report.md, ledger.sqlite, promote.py, grading/, bench/ and costs.csv.
1. Enumerate every claim: pass rates, promotions, benchmark comparisons, savings and compliance. Mark each one verified (with a SQL query or file reference), unverified, or false.
2. Recompute the per-class pass rates and Wilson intervals from ledger.sqlite and diff them against the report.
3. Rerun promote.py on the ledger and check that the promotions match.
4. Check blindness: grep the grader prompts for model and tier names, and recompute kappa.

mission: Make one legacy tool that you or a client are licensed to use agent-drivable, lawfully, and decide honestly whether wrapping it is an arbitrage or a consulting treadmill. The pieces are an agent-built command-line wrapper covering the tool's top five real actions, each using the most stable lawful mechanism (a documented API or file format before UI automation), wrapped as an MCP server, with a written legal basis per action. Done means every action passes a 50-run reliability replay, survives a simulated vendor update, has its maintenance cost measured, and the falsifier has a verdict: more than one breakage per vendor update per month means it is a consulting gig, not arbitrage.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A systems-integration engineer would refuse to drive a UI by clicking if a documented interface exists, because clicks are the most brittle and legally fraught path. They would look, in order, for a documented API, an export or import file format, a local database, or a config file, and only fall back to screen automation for the actions that have none. They would get written authorization from the software owner, and they would document the legal basis for each interop method, leaning on the interoperability provisions of copyright law (in the US, the DMCA Section 1201(f) interoperability exception and the idea that interface facts are not themselves protected) rather than assuming it is fine. They would build a regression harness so a breaking vendor update is caught the same day, and measure the breakage rate before pricing a service on it.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The target tool you are licensed to use: its documentation, its export/import formats, its local database or config files, and its official API if one exists. The vendor's terms of service and your license agreement, which say what automation and interoperability are permitted. The legal texts: the DMCA Section 1201(f) interoperability exception and your jurisdiction's equivalent. For stubborn native binaries, the publicly documented, lawful study of software for interoperability, keeping to clean behavioral reconstruction rather than copying protected code, as @lizthedeveloper lays out (engine re-implementation and functional reconstruction are the defensible routes; shipping recovered original source is not).
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: A tiered interop strategy: documented API first, then file formats (read/write the tool's own export and import), then local DB access (SQLite or similar), then config files, and UI automation only as the last resort for actions with no other path. An agent-built CLI that exposes each action as a subcommand, following @catlabs' 'build yourself a CLI tool to interact with X'. An MCP server wrapping the CLI for discovery and auth. A reliability harness running each action 50 times and recording the success rate. A vendor-update simulation (pin the current version, then test against an updated or mutated interface). gitmcp/gitingest/deepwiki for repo comprehension. A breakage log for the maintenance-cost measurement.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A 50-run replay per action with a success-rate threshold (for example 98%) that is not met by UI-automation actions as often as by API or file-format actions, which is itself the finding. A vendor-update simulation that the wrapper survives, or does not. A week of real tasks run through the MCP server with a logged error count. A written legal-basis sheet reviewed against the license and the interoperability exception. The pre-registered falsifier: breakage more than once per vendor update per month means the maintenance cost eats the margin and it is a consulting engagement, not an arbitrage.

one_shot:
ROLE
You are a systems-integration engineer who makes licensed software agent-drivable, lawfully, and measures reliability before anyone prices a service on it. You reach for a documented interface before you ever drive a UI.

CONTEXT
The saved posts describe the opportunity and its guardrail.
- @catlabs: when a tool has no MCP, tell the agent 'Build yourself a CLI tool to interact with X'. MCP is best for auth, discovery and distribution; a custom CLI wins for bespoke deep control and uses fewer tokens. Expect security flags.
- @theericmichaud and @backsla.sh: 'Reverse Engineer Anything' and an MCP with a Ghidra backend, used to understand how software works and to revive unsupported hardware, 'on software you are authorized to analyze'.
- @chase.h.ai: pointing a coding agent at a device on your own network to reconfigure it.
- @zchangd and @atlasberry008: the demand - workflows over legacy business software, and Chamath's claim that software IP stops being a moat once services go headless and agents call them via MCP.
- @tom__shipley: Bending Spoons buys stagnant software and rebuilds the core lean - the business value of making legacy tools cheap to operate.
- @lizthedeveloper: which reconstruction methods stay legal - engine re-implementation and functional reconstruction are defensible; shipping recovered original source is not; comparing behavior gives an automatic test oracle.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Authorization first. Only target software you or your client are licensed to use, and only methods the license and terms permit. Write the legal basis per action before coding. If authorization is unclear, stop and ask.
- Stable before brittle. For each action, use a documented API, then a file format, then a local DB, then config, and UI automation only as a last resort. Record which tier each action uses.
- Lawful interoperability only. Lean on the DMCA Section 1201(f) interoperability provision and the fact that interface facts are not protected. Do not copy protected code into your output; reconstruct behavior cleanly.
- Do not target third-party systems you are not authorized to touch, and do not defeat access controls protecting someone else's data.

DELIVERABLES
1. authorization.md: the license and terms clauses permitting automation and interoperability, and a legal-basis line per action.
2. actions.md: the top five real actions, and for each the chosen interop tier (API, file, DB, config, UI) with why.
3. cli/: the agent-built command-line wrapper, one subcommand per action.
4. mcp/: the CLI wrapped as an MCP server for auth and discovery.
5. reliability.csv: 50 runs per action, success rate, and a vendor-update simulation result.
6. maintenance.md: a week of real tasks, the breakage log, and the cost estimate.
7. report.md with the arbitrage-versus-consulting verdict.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List actions that only work via brittle UI automation, actions whose legal basis is uncertain, interfaces you could not find documentation for, and reliability numbers below threshold. Fill what you can: find the file format, read the docs. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Is every action on something I am licensed to automate? How many actions need UI clicking versus data access? Would a vendor update break this? Is the maintenance cost under the falsifier threshold?

STOP
Stop when the five actions are wrapped, replayed 50 times each, and survive (or fail) the update simulation. Stop and ask if authorization for any action is unclear, or if the only path defeats an access control.

RETURN
Return authorization.md, actions.md, cli/, mcp/, reliability.csv, maintenance.md and report.md with the sections Authorization, Actions, Reliability, Maintenance, Verdict and Gaps.

steps.title: Confirm authorization and write the legal basis
steps.goal: Establish that the tool and the methods are ones you are licensed to use, before any code.
steps.prompt:
Identify the target: one tool you or a client are licensed to use that lacks an MCP, such as a legacy desktop scheduler, an old ERP or a desktop accounting suite.
Read the license agreement and the vendor's terms of service. Quote the clauses that govern automation, API use and interoperability. If they forbid automation, stop here and report that.
Write authorization.md stating: the licensed user, the clauses permitting (or limiting) automation, and the legal basis you will rely on for interoperability work, such as the DMCA Section 1201(f) interoperability exception in the US and the principle that interface facts are not copyrightable.
State plainly that this work targets only software the user is licensed to operate and never defeats access controls protecting other parties' data.
If the target is a network device, confirm it is the user's own device on the user's own network.
steps.expect: authorization.md with quoted license and terms clauses, the named interoperability legal basis, and the scope statement.
steps.audit: Confirm the quoted clauses actually permit the planned automation. If any clause is ambiguous, mark that action as needing legal review and do not build it yet. Fail if authorization.md asserts a right without quoting the clause, or if the target is not clearly licensed to the user.

steps.title: Map the five actions to the most stable lawful interface
steps.goal: Choose, per action, the least brittle legitimate mechanism.
steps.prompt:
List the top five real actions the user performs in the tool, from their actual workflow, not a feature tour.
For each action, investigate interfaces in this order and pick the first that works:
1. A documented official API.
2. The tool's own export/import file formats (read what it writes, write what it reads).
3. Its local database (for example a SQLite file) or data files, read directly.
4. Its config files.
5. UI automation, only if none of the above exists for that action.
Use gitingest, deepwiki and gitmcp to understand any open repos or SDKs you are allowed to read, following @ariacodez.
Record in actions.md the chosen tier per action and why, and count how many of the five require UI automation versus direct data access. That count is an early read on how brittle and how maintainable the wrapper will be.
steps.expect: actions.md: five actions, each with its interop tier, the evidence it works, and the UI-versus-data count.
steps.audit: For each action claimed to use an API or file format, confirm with a single successful read or call before trusting it. If more than two of five actions fall back to UI automation, flag the project as high-maintenance up front. Fail if any action's tier was chosen without a working probe.

steps.title: Agent-build the CLI
steps.goal: Produce a command-line wrapper exposing the five actions.
steps.prompt:
Have the agent build a CLI, @catlabs-style: 'build yourself a CLI tool to interact with [the tool]', one subcommand per action.
Each subcommand uses the interop tier chosen in step 2. API-backed and file-backed subcommands should be pure data operations with no UI dependency. UI-automation subcommands are isolated in their own module so their brittleness is contained.
Make every subcommand idempotent where possible and give it a dry-run mode that shows what it would do without doing it.
Add structured logging: each invocation records the action, the tier, inputs (redacting any secret or personal data), the result and the duration.
Write unit tests that run against a sandbox copy or test account of the tool, never against live production data.
Keep tokens low by preferring the CLI's compact output over large tool schemas, as @catlabs notes.
steps.expect: cli/ with five subcommands, a dry-run mode, structured logging, and tests against a sandbox.
steps.audit: Run each subcommand's dry-run and confirm it describes the right action. Confirm no secret or personal data is written to logs. Confirm the tests use a sandbox, not production. Fail if a UI-automation subcommand is entangled with the data-backed ones, since that spreads brittleness.

steps.title: Wrap the CLI as an MCP server
steps.goal: Expose the actions to an agent with proper auth and discovery.
steps.prompt:
Wrap the CLI as an MCP server, which @catlabs and @atlasberry008 note is the right layer for authentication, discovery and distribution, even though the CLI does the work.
Each action becomes an MCP tool with a typed schema and a clear description of what it does and its blast radius.
Authentication reads credentials from the environment or a secret store at call time, never hard-coded, and the server never logs credential values.
Mark write or destructive actions as requiring explicit confirmation, so an agent cannot silently mutate the user's data.
Add a capability manifest so a calling agent can discover the five actions and their constraints.
Test the server with a real agent performing one safe read action end to end.
steps.expect: mcp/ with a server exposing five typed tools, environment-based auth, confirmation gating on writes, and an end-to-end read test.
steps.audit: Confirm destructive tools require confirmation and cannot run unattended by default. Confirm no credential value appears in logs by grepping by pattern without printing. Fail if any write action is exposed without a confirmation gate.

steps.title: Reliability replay and vendor-update simulation
steps.goal: Measure how often each action works and whether an update breaks it.
steps.prompt:
Run each of the five actions 50 times against the sandbox, varying inputs realistically. Record the success rate per action in reliability.csv.
Expect API-backed and file-backed actions to be near-perfect and UI-automation actions to be flakier. That gap is a finding, not a nuisance.
Simulate a vendor update: change the version, or mutate the interface the brittle actions depend on (rename a UI element, shift an export column), and re-run the replay. Record which actions survive and which break.
Set a pass threshold (for example 98% success) and mark each action pass or fail.
For any action below threshold, note whether a more stable tier is available that you skipped.
steps.expect: reliability.csv with per-action success rates before and after the simulated update, and a pass/fail per action.
steps.audit: Confirm the 50 runs used varied inputs, not the same call repeated. If a UI action passed the first replay but broke under the update simulation, record both numbers. Fail if the update simulation was not run, since it is the whole point of the maintainability question.

steps.title: Measure maintenance cost over a real week
steps.goal: Price the service honestly by watching it break.
steps.prompt:
Run a week of the user's real tasks through the MCP server (on their own licensed instance, with their approval).
Log every breakage: which action, what changed, how long the fix took.
Estimate the maintenance cost: breakages per week, hours per fix, and how that scales across the number of client instances a service would cover.
Tie it to @tom__shipley's Bending Spoons point: the value is in rebuilding and operating a core cheaply, so the question is whether operating this wrapper is cheap or a treadmill.
Compute the falsifier metric directly: breakages per vendor update per month. If it exceeds one, the maintenance eats the margin.
Record which actions caused the most breakage, since those are the ones to move to a more stable tier or drop.
steps.expect: maintenance.md with the week's breakage log, hours per fix, the per-update breakage rate, and a scaling estimate.
steps.audit: Confirm the week ran on a licensed instance with the user's approval, not against any third-party system. If the week was quiet by luck (no vendor update landed), say so and treat the update simulation as the maintainability evidence instead. Fail if the falsifier metric is not computed.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Deliver the arbitrage-versus-consulting verdict with the legal basis and gaps.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) Per-action reliability: the 50-run success rate against the threshold.
(b) The vendor-update simulation result per action.
(c) The real-week error count through the MCP server.
(d) The legal-basis sheet, reviewed against the license and the interoperability exception.
(e) The falsifier: is breakage more than once per vendor update per month? If so, state plainly this is a consulting engagement priced hourly, not an arbitrage priced as a flat 'we run it for you' service.
Write report.md with the sections Authorization, Actions, Reliability, Maintenance, Verdict and Gaps. State which actions are robust (API/file-backed) and which are fragile (UI-backed), and whether the wrapper is worth selling as a service. Rank the gaps by impact on reliability and legal exposure.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a ranked gap list.
steps.audit: Any 'robust' claim without a 50-run number is downgraded. Any action without a legal basis is flagged, not shipped. Confirm the report never claims a right to automate software the user is not licensed for. Fail if the Verdict does not state the falsifier result.

gap_audit_prompt:

7. Confirm nothing targets a third-party system or defeats an access control protecting others' data.
8. Rank the gaps by reliability and legal exposure, fix the top three, and report what you could not fix.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps' and an A-F grade on whether the wrapper is a sellable arbitrage.
self_questions: Is every action targeting software the user is actually licensed to use and automate?
Did I quote the license and terms clauses, or just assume automation is allowed?
How many of the five actions need UI automation versus direct API or file access?
For each UI-automation action, did a documented interface exist that I skipped?
Would a realistic vendor update break any action, and which ones?
Is the per-update breakage rate under the falsifier's one-per-month threshold?
Are write and destructive actions gated behind explicit confirmation in the MCP server?
Did any credential or personal data reach a log?
Is my interoperability legal basis sound, or am I overreading the exception?
Does anything here touch a third-party system or access control I am not authorized for?

A real week of tasks through the MCP server on a licensed instance, with a logged breakage count.

mission: Build one scheduled defensive agent that runs the public-footprint toolkit against your own identities, never anyone else's, and files the remediation. The pieces are a weekly job that runs username and email enumeration on your own handles, a photo pass that sends your own recent public images to a geolocation model and flags any that resolve near home, a diff against the prior run, and auto-drafted (never auto-submitted) data-broker opt-out requests. Done means the job is scheduled with an identity allowlist that makes targeting anyone else impossible, results are stored dated, and a month of runs has tested the falsifier.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A privacy engineer or a personal-threat-model consultant would start from a written threat model, not a tool list: who the adversary is (an ex, a stalker, a doxxing mob, a data broker), what they already have, and what single new fact would cause real harm. They would run the offensive tools only against identities the subject owns and consents to, under an explicit allowlist, because running them against third parties is harassment and often illegal. They would treat geolocation as a leak test on the subject's own photos, measure the error radius, and prioritize removals by harm, not by count. They would prefer authoritative removal routes (state privacy-law requests, the credit-bureau freeze, platform takedowns) over broker-by-broker whack-a-mole.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Your own account list and email addresses. Your own last 20 public images with their EXIF stripped and kept, so you can compare what the model infers against the truth. The California CCPA/CPRA and equivalent deletion-request templates. The three nationwide credit bureaus' freeze pages. The data-broker opt-out directory maintained by privacy groups such as the EFF and Privacy Rights Clearinghouse. The relevant platforms' own 'download your data' exports, which show what is actually public. Sherlock's site-list JSON, so you know its false-positive rate. GeoSpy's and any open geolocation model's stated accuracy.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Sherlock via uv (uv venv, uv pip install sherlock-project) and a second username engine to cross-check coverage and false positives. An email-exposure check against Have I Been Pwned's API for your own addresses only. A geolocation pass on your own images with a documented error radius, scored as 'resolves within N km of a sensitive location'. A SQLite table keyed by date for diffing. A scheduler (cron or a systemd timer) with an identity allowlist enforced in code. Opt-out requests drafted into a review queue, submitted only by a human. Archive checks for your own deleted content, to know what persists.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A measured false-positive rate for the username tools: how many flagged accounts are actually yours, confirmed by login or by you. The geolocation error radius on your own images where you know the true location, which tells you whether the leak is real. Confirmation emails from brokers that a removal completed, re-checked 30 and 60 days later for reappearance. A credit freeze confirmed at all three bureaus. The pre-registered falsifier: three consecutive weekly runs that surface nothing new, after which a quarterly manual check is enough.
