6. schedule: a cron or systemd timer entry, and a kill switch.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List the username hits you could not confirm are actually the operator's, the photos with no known ground-truth location (so the error radius is unknown), the brokers with no opt-out route found, and any platform whose public exposure you could not read. Fill what you can. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Is every target on the allowlist? What is the geolocation error radius on photos where I know the truth? Which hit, if real, enables the most damaging fact from the threat model? Am I about to submit a form a human should approve?

STOP
Stop after one full run plus the drafted queue. Stop immediately and refuse if any requested target is not the operator's own identity.

RETURN
Return threat_model.md, allowlist.yaml, guard.py, sentinel.py, the SQLite store, remediation/ and schedule/, plus report.md with the sections Threat Model, Findings, Leak Radius, Remediation Queue and Gaps.

steps.title: Threat model and identity allowlist
steps.goal: Define who and what you are defending against, and make targeting anyone else impossible.
steps.prompt:
Before any tool runs, write threat_model.md. Name the realistic adversary (an ex-partner, a stalker, a harassment mob, a data broker reselling to anyone). State what they plausibly already know. State the single new fact that would cause real harm, usually a current home address, a child's school or a daily pattern. List the sensitive locations to protect.
Then create allowlist.yaml holding only the operator's own handles, email addresses and local image folders. Write guard.py so every later tool call passes its target through it and raises on anything not listed.
Write a test that feeds guard.py a handle and an image path that are not on the allowlist and confirms both are refused and logged.
State in the header, in plain language, that this system runs only against the operator's own identities and must never be pointed at a third party.
steps.expect: threat_model.md, allowlist.yaml, guard.py and a passing refusal test.
steps.audit: Try to run a downstream tool with a target absent from the allowlist. It must refuse. If guard.py can be bypassed by calling a tool directly, route every tool through it before continuing. Fail if the allowlist is empty or the refusal test passes a non-listed target.

steps.title: Username enumeration with false-positive control
steps.goal: Find the operator's own accounts across the web and measure the tools' error rate.
steps.prompt:
Install Sherlock with uv: uv venv, source the venv, uv pip install sherlock-project. Run sherlock on each allowlisted handle, passing several at once.
Run a second username engine, such as Alien's Eye, on the same handles, since @declan.middleton claims wider coverage. Compare the two result sets.
Every handle must come from allowlist.yaml through guard.py.
For each hit, record the site, the URL and a confidence flag. Then measure the false-positive rate: sample 20 hits and have the operator confirm which are actually theirs. Sherlock matches by URL pattern and over-reports, so this rate matters.
Store results in the accounts table keyed by run date. Record which sites each tool covers that the other misses, so you know your true coverage, not just one tool's view. Note any account you had forgotten you owned, because dormant accounts with old passwords are prime targets.
steps.expect: accounts.csv per run, a union-and-intersection comparison of the two tools, and a measured false-positive rate.
steps.audit: Confirm every queried handle was on the allowlist by checking guard.py's log. If the false-positive rate is above 30%, down-weight single-tool hits and require confirmation before any hit drives a remediation draft. Fail if any non-operator handle was queried.

steps.title: Email exposure on your own addresses
steps.goal: See which breaches and accounts expose the operator's own emails.
steps.prompt:
For each allowlisted email address, check exposure against the Have I Been Pwned API. Read the API key from the environment and never print it.
Record each breach: name, date, and the data classes exposed (passwords, addresses, phone numbers).
Query only the operator's own addresses, enforced through guard.py.
Map each breached address to the accounts found in step 2 where they overlap, so a single compromised password can be traced to the accounts it threatens.
Do not attempt any dark-web crawl or third-party email lookup. The scope is the operator's own addresses and public breach data only.
Flag any breach that exposed a security answer or a current address, because those feed the threat model's most-damaging-fact directly.
steps.expect: breaches.csv keyed by address and date, and an overlap map to the step 2 accounts.
steps.audit: Confirm the API key never appears in logs or output by grepping for it by pattern without printing it. Confirm only allowlisted addresses were queried. Fail if any third-party address was checked, or if a breach list has no dates.

steps.title: Geolocation leak test on your own photos
steps.goal: Measure whether the operator's own public images reveal a sensitive location.
steps.prompt:
Collect the operator's last 20 public images (from their own posts or 'download your data' export). Keep a copy of the original EXIF separately, then send EXIF-stripped copies to a geolocation model such as GeoSpy or an open equivalent, as @innovation describes: inference from buildings, plants, street layout and shadows.
For each image where the true location is known, compute the error radius between the model's guess and the truth. This tells you whether the leak is real or the model is guessing.
Flag any image that resolves within N km (set N from the threat model, for example 2 km) of a sensitive location.
All images come from the allowlisted folders through guard.py. Do not geolocate anyone else's photos.
Record, per image, the predicted location, the error radius and whether it breaches a sensitive zone.
steps.expect: geo.csv with predicted location, error radius and breach flag per image, and a short leak summary.
steps.audit: Confirm the error radius is computed only where ground truth exists, and that images with unknown truth are marked, not scored as safe. If the model's median error exceeds the flag radius, state that the geolocation signal is too weak to act on for this set. Fail if any non-operator image was processed.

steps.title: Diff, prioritize and draft remediation
steps.goal: Turn new findings into a prioritized, human-approved removal queue.
steps.prompt:
Diff this run against the previous run in the SQLite store. New accounts, new breaches and new geo-flags are the actionable set.
Prioritize by harm, not count: a hit that enables the threat model's most-damaging fact ranks above a dormant forum account.
For each prioritized hit, draft the remediation into remediation/queue/, never submitting it:
- A CCPA/CPRA deletion request for data brokers, from a template, pre-filled with the operator's details.
- A platform takedown or account-deletion note where an old account is exposed.
- A one-time checklist for the three-bureau credit freeze and recovery-code storage, from @lizthedeveloper's checklist.
Each draft states what it targets, the legal basis and where the human submits it.
Leave submission to the operator. The agent files drafts only.
steps.expect: remediation/queue/ with one drafted request per prioritized hit, ranked, plus a one-time freeze checklist.
steps.audit: Confirm nothing was submitted: no network POST to a broker form appears in the logs. Confirm each draft cites a legal basis and a submission location. Fail if a low-harm hit outranks a threat-model-critical one, or if any request was auto-sent.

steps.title: Schedule, diff loop and kill switch
steps.goal: Run the sentinel weekly, unattended and safely.
steps.prompt:
Wrap sentinel.py in a weekly cron or systemd timer. On each run it re-checks the allowlist, runs steps 2 to 4, diffs against the last run, appends dated rows and refreshes the remediation queue.
Follow the DB-and-cron loop pattern (@angus.sewell, after Boris Cherny's 'build systems that prompt your AI'): a jobs table, a run that detects new findings, and skills that scope, draft and queue, stopping at the human-approval gate.
Add a kill switch: a flag file or a single command that disables the timer, for when the operator is traveling and locations change.
Write run outputs to dated files so three consecutive empty runs are easy to see.
Do not escalate scope over time. The allowlist is fixed unless the operator edits it by hand.
steps.expect: schedule/ with the timer unit or crontab line, a jobs table, and a documented kill switch.
steps.audit: Dry-run the timer and confirm it re-validates the allowlist on every run. Confirm the kill switch actually stops it. Fail if the scheduled job can add targets on its own, or if it submits anything without the human gate.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Confirm the leaks are real, the removals stick, and test the falsifier.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) Username false-positive rate: the share of flagged accounts the operator confirms are theirs.
(b) Geolocation error radius on known-truth photos, and whether any real leak remains.
(c) Broker removals: confirmation emails, re-checked at 30 and 60 days for reappearance.
(d) The credit freeze confirmed at all three bureaus.
(e) The falsifier: have three consecutive weekly runs surfaced nothing new? If so, recommend dropping to quarterly.
Write report.md with the sections Threat Model, Findings, Leak Radius, Remediation Status, Falsifier and Gaps. State plainly which exposures are confirmed real versus tool noise, and which removals are verified versus pending. Rank the remaining gaps by harm. Include a short 'what changed since last month' line so the operator can see the trend at a glance. Note explicitly which exposures are already fixed and should drop off next run.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a prioritized gap list.
steps.audit: Any 'removed' broker without a confirmation email is downgraded to pending. Any geo-flag without a measured radius is downgraded to unverified. Confirm the report never names a third party as a target. Fail if the falsifier section is missing.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are an independent privacy reviewer. Open report.md, threat_model.md, allowlist.yaml, guard.py, the SQLite store and remediation/.
1. First and hardest: confirm every target ever queried is on the allowlist and belongs to the operator. Grep guard.py's log for any target not in allowlist.yaml. If one exists, stop and flag it as a serious violation.
2. Enumerate every finding claim: accounts, breaches, geo-flags, removals. Mark each verified, unverified or false.
3. Recompute the username false-positive rate and the geolocation error radius from the stored data.
4. Check that no remediation was auto-submitted: look for outbound POSTs to broker or platform forms.
5. Check for secret leakage: search logs for API-key-shaped strings by pattern without printing any match.
6. Check prioritization: is the queue ranked by threat-model harm, not by count?
7. List what is missing: unconfirmed hits, photos with no ground truth, brokers with no route, removals not re-checked at 30 and 60 days.
8. Rank gaps by harm. Fix the top three now. Report what you could not fix and why.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps', and a one-line statement confirming no third party was targeted.
self_questions: Is every handle, email, image and plate on the allowlist and owned by the operator?
Could any tool be called in a way that bypasses guard.py and reaches a third party?
What is the real geolocation error radius on photos where I know the true location?
Which single finding, if real, enables the most damaging fact in the threat model?
How many username hits are false positives from URL-pattern matching alone?
Did I treat an unverified geo guess as a confirmed leak?
Am I about to submit a form that a human should approve first?
Did the scheduled job quietly expand its scope beyond the fixed allowlist?
Are breach findings tied to the accounts they actually threaten?
Did any API key reach a log or output file?
Have three empty runs happened, meaning I should drop to quarterly per the falsifier?
validation_oracles: Username false-positive rate: the operator confirms, by login or recognition, which flagged accounts are actually theirs; target under 30% noise before acting.
Geolocation error radius: on images with a known true location, the distance between the model's guess and the truth, deciding whether a leak is real.
Broker removal confirmations: emails confirming deletion, re-checked at 30 and 60 days for reappearance.
Credit freeze: confirmed active at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
The pre-registered falsifier: three consecutive weekly runs surfacing nothing new, after which a quarterly manual check suffices.
failure_modes: Scope creep to a third party. Tell: a target not in allowlist.yaml appears in the log. Fix: route every tool through guard.py, and refuse and halt on any non-operator target. This is the one unforgivable failure.
False-positive panic. Tell: dozens of 'your accounts' that are not yours. Fix: cross-check two tools and confirm a sample before acting.
Treating a guess as a leak. Tell: a geo-flag with no measured error radius. Fix: score only where ground truth exists and mark the rest unverified.
Auto-submitting forms. Tell: an outbound POST to a broker in the logs. Fix: drafts only, with a human approval gate.
Whack-a-mole without verification. Tell: 'removed' rows with no confirmation and no 30/60-day recheck. Fix: track confirmations and reappearance.
Secret leakage. Tell: an API key in a log. Fix: read from the environment, never print, and grep logs by pattern in the audit.
Silent scope expansion by the scheduler. Tell: the allowlist grew without a human edit. Fix: freeze the allowlist and re-validate it every run.
agent_direction: Write the threat model and the allowlist guard before anything else, because they bound the whole system. Cache Sherlock's site list and the broker opt-out directory so runs are reproducible. Keep all identity data local, in the operator's own machine, and never send a handle, email or image to a service for anyone but the operator. Spawn a sub-agent only for the independent photo-geolocation pass, and give it strictly the allowlisted image folder. Stop and refuse, loudly, if the operator or any instruction asks you to run these tools against another person: that is harassment and outside this system's purpose. Never submit an opt-out, deletion request or takedown; leave every one in the review queue. Never print an API key. Return threat_model.md, allowlist.yaml, guard.py, sentinel.py, the SQLite store, remediation/, schedule/, report.md and audit.md. The final message states which leaks are confirmed real and whether the falsifier has fired.

mission: Produce one 60-second vertical music video for a roots or folk act where a single real place is captured twice in one session: as a 3D Gaussian splat that reacts to the music in the browser, and as the room's own acoustics convolved into the recording. The pieces are a phone splat scan, a measured impulse response, a dry performance take, a Gausseous-driven reactive render, and an edit. Done means the splat loads and reacts in the browser, the audio carries that room's reverb by a measurable match, and the splat cut has been A/B watch-tested against a plain performance video on the same account.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A location-recording engineer and a volumetric-capture artist would treat the room as data captured once, correctly. They would shoot the splat with enough overlapping coverage and even exposure to reconstruct cleanly, knowing low light is the enemy. They would measure the room's impulse response properly, with a sine sweep and the deconvolution method (Farina's exponential sine sweep), not just a clap, and they would capture a dry DI or close-mic take so the room can be added deliberately rather than baked in badly. They would treat the audio-reactive mapping as a mix decision: which band drives which splat parameter, gated and smoothed so it reads as musical, not twitchy. And they would test watch-through, because a format that loses the viewer is a failed format.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The actual room: a porch, a church, a barn, the 200-year-old Girardeau House that @chancemccoymusic plays for its resonance. A phone with a splat app (Polycam or Luma) producing a .ply or .splat. A sine-sweep file and a recording of the swept response, for a measured impulse response. A dry, close-miked or DI performance take, uncolored by the room. The Lomax field-recording tradition (@dimestoreradio, Nimrod Workman filmed at home) as the model: place and song captured together. Gausseous (github.com/quixbrics/gausseous) and its SparkJS renderer. The khaen or another drone instrument for sustained tones that make the reactivity readable.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Phone Gaussian-splat capture (Polycam or Luma), exported as .ply or .splat. Impulse-response measurement by exponential sine sweep and deconvolution (Python with numpy and scipy, or Room EQ Wizard), producing a convolution reverb IR. A DAW with a convolution reverb (such as a free IR loader) to apply that IR to the dry take. Gausseous in the browser for audio-reactive rendering, depth of field, lens curvature and film emulation, with the reactivity mapped per frequency band using the Web Audio AnalyserNode. A 2-hour-safe render-export path. A/B testing on one platform with matched posting times.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The .splat opens and reacts in Gausseous in a desktop browser at an acceptable frame rate, with no missing-geometry holes in the performance area. The convolution match: the reverb decay time (RT60) of the processed dry take within about 10% of the RT60 measured from the room's impulse response. A blind listening test where people match the processed audio to the room better than chance. The A/B watch-through and completion rate of the splat cut versus a plain performance video, over matched posts. The falsifier: if interior scans are too noisy to read, or the splat cut loses watch-through, the format is a gimmick.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt:
You are a location-recording engineer and a volumetric-capture artist making one roots-music video. Capture one real room twice in a single session.
1. Scan the room as a Gaussian splat with a phone (Polycam or Luma). Shoot for even, overlapping coverage so the performance area has no holes.
2. In the same session, measure the room's impulse response with an exponential sine sweep and deconvolution, and record a dry, close-miked performance take.
3. Convolve the dry take with the measured IR so the recording carries that room's acoustics. Check that the processed RT60 is within 10% of the measured RT60.
4. Load the .splat into Gausseous and map audio-reactivity per frequency band (bass drives scale, highs drive shimmer), gated and smoothed so it reads musically. Use a drone instrument for sustained, readable tones.
5. Cut a 60-second vertical piece intercutting real performance footage with the reacting splat.
6. A/B it against a plain performance video on the same account, matched for posting time, and report watch-through and completion.
Return the splat, the IR, the processed audio, the Gausseous project, the edit, and the A/B result with the falsifier verdict.

one_shot:
ROLE
You are a location-recording engineer and a volumetric-capture artist. You capture a place correctly once, then build both the sound and the image from that one capture.

CONTEXT
- @chancemccoymusic tests the resonance of the 200-year-old Girardeau House, treating the walls as part of the instrument.
- @dimestoreradio: Alan Lomax filmed Nimrod and Molly Workman singing at home in 1983. Place and song, recorded together.
- @murphydoesnotmatter: a tune filmed at The Palace in Yancey County, the kind of specific room worth scanning.
- @6ab3 and @gerrylistudio: TouchDesigner, MediaPipe and Gaussian splats, including Polycam scanning.
- @peppes_ghost: a DIY Raspberry Pi LiDAR scanner for rooms and caves where phone photogrammetry struggles.
- @dave_bewick: Gausseous, a free browser tool that makes splats audio-reactive with depth of field, lens curvature, film emulation and render export, built on World Labs' SparkJS.
- @howtown_videos: DeepPIV sweeps a laser sheet through a transparent creature to reconstruct it in 3D, a reference for volumetric glowing forms.
- @pop.music.culture: the khaen, a free-reed instrument that sustains drones on both inhale and exhale.
- @honeycrush.online: a folk-horror video shot DIY by two people with one camera, proof the audience accepts small-crew music videos.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- One place, one session. The splat scan, the impulse response and the dry performance take all come from the same room on the same day.
- The audio must carry the room's measured acoustics, not a generic reverb preset.
- Get permission to scan the room, and name the place and musicians honestly. This is documentary, not synthetic: no generated faces.
- The reactivity must read as musical. Gate and smooth it.

DELIVERABLES
1. capture/: the phone splat as .ply or .splat, a coverage note, the sine-sweep recording, the deconvolved impulse response (IR), and the dry performance take.
2. audio/: the dry take convolved with the IR, plus a measurement showing the processed RT60 against the room's measured RT60.
3. render/: a Gausseous project loading the splat, with a per-band reactivity map (which band drives scale, position, shimmer), gated and smoothed, and an exported clip.
4. edit/: a 60-second vertical cut intercutting real performance footage with the reacting splat.
5. ab_test/: the plain-performance control video, the posting plan matched for time of day, and a metrics sheet for watch-through and completion.
6. report.md.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List the parts of the scan with holes or noise (low light is the usual cause), whether the IR was a proper sweep or only a clap, whether a dry take exists or the room was baked in, and whether the A/B has enough views to read. Fill what you can: rescan in better light, redo the sweep. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Does the splat have holes where the performer stands? Is the reverb the real room, measured, or a preset? Does the reactivity read as musical or twitchy? Does the splat cut hold the viewer as long as the plain video?

STOP
Stop when the splat reacts in-browser, the audio carries the measured room, and the A/B has run on matched posts. Stop and ask before posting publicly on the act's account.

RETURN
Return capture/, audio/, render/, edit/, ab_test/ and report.md with the sections Capture, Acoustics, Render, Edit, A/B Result and Gaps.

steps.title: Scan the room and measure its sound
steps.goal: Capture one place as both a clean splat and a measured impulse response, in one session.
steps.prompt:
At the chosen room (a porch, church, barn or resonant old house like the Girardeau House), do three captures in one session.
(1) Splat scan with Polycam or Luma on a phone. Move slowly in overlapping passes, keep exposure even, and over-cover the area where the performer will stand. Export .ply or .splat. Where phone photogrammetry struggles in low light or large caves, note the @peppes_ghost DIY LiDAR option as a fallback.
(2) Impulse response: play an exponential sine sweep through a speaker and record it with a flat mic at the performer's position. You will deconvolve this into an IR.
(3) Dry performance take: record the instrument and voice close-miked or DI, so the room is not already baked into the sound.
Log the room name, permission, lighting and mic positions.
steps.expect: capture/ with the .splat, the sweep recording, the dry take, and capture_notes.md covering coverage, lighting and positions.
steps.audit: Open the .splat in a viewer. If the performance area has holes or heavy noise, rescan in better light before continuing. Confirm the dry take has minimal room sound. Fail if the IR is only a clap when a sweep was possible, or if no dry take exists.

steps.title: Deconvolve the impulse response
steps.goal: Turn the sweep into a usable convolution reverb IR with a measured RT60.
steps.prompt:
Deconvolve the recorded sweep against the reference sweep to recover the room's impulse response, using Farina's exponential-sine-sweep method. Do it in Python with numpy and scipy, or in Room EQ Wizard.
From the IR, compute the room's RT60 (the time for the energy to decay 60 dB, usually via the T30 or T20 extrapolation from the Schroeder integral).
Save the IR as a WAV ready for a convolution reverb.
Inspect the IR for artifacts: a clean exponential decay, no pre-ringing, no clipping in the sweep recording.
Record the RT60 and the IR length. This measured RT60 is the target the processed audio must match later. Keep the reference sweep file and the recorded sweep together, labeled, so the deconvolution is reproducible. Note the speaker and mic used, since the IR carries their coloration and you may want to compensate.
steps.expect: capture/room_ir.wav, a plot of the IR and its decay curve, and the measured RT60 value.
steps.audit: Check the sweep recording for clipping before trusting the IR. If the decay curve is not roughly linear in dB, the measurement is contaminated, so remeasure. Fail if RT60 cannot be computed or the IR shows pre-ringing from a bad deconvolution.

steps.title: Convolve the room into the recording
steps.goal: Make the dry take carry the real room's acoustics and verify the match.
steps.prompt:
Load the dry performance take into a DAW with a convolution reverb, or convolve in Python (scipy.signal.fftconvolve), using capture/room_ir.wav.
Balance the dry and wet signal so the result sounds like the performance happened in that room, not drowned in reverb.
Then verify: measure the RT60 of the processed take (from a decaying note or by analysis) and compare it with the room's measured RT60 from step 2. They should agree within about 10%.
If you have a wet reference recording of the same performance in the room, compare the convolved version to it as a second check.
Export the processed audio. Keep both the dry and the processed takes, so the edit can choose. Note the wet/dry ratio you settled on, because it is the single biggest taste decision here and you will want to recall it for the next room.
steps.expect: audio/performance_room.wav and a short match report: processed RT60 versus measured RT60, with the percentage difference.
steps.audit: If the processed RT60 differs from the measured room by more than 10%, re-check the wet/dry balance and the IR normalization. Fail if a generic reverb preset was used instead of the measured IR, or if the match report is missing.

steps.title: Make the splat react to the music
steps.goal: Load the splat into Gausseous and drive it musically from the audio.
steps.prompt:
Load the .splat into Gausseous (quixbrics.github.io/gausseous). Confirm it renders without holes in the performance area.
Use the Web Audio AnalyserNode to split the processed audio into bands. Map them deliberately: bass drives overall scale or a slow pulse, mids drive position drift, highs drive shimmer or point size. Gate each mapping with a threshold and smooth it with an attack/release envelope so the motion reads as musical rather than twitchy.
Use a sustained, droning passage, like the khaen or a bowed note, to tune the response, because long tones make reactivity legible.
Add Gausseous's depth of field, a little lens curvature and film emulation for the volumetric glow in the DeepPIV reference, without burying the room.
Export a reactive clip at least as long as the final edit.
steps.expect: render/ with the Gausseous project or settings, a per-band reactivity map, and an exported reactive clip.
steps.audit: Watch the clip against the audio. If the motion looks random or disconnected from the beat, raise the gates and lengthen the smoothing. Confirm no missing-geometry holes show in frame. Fail if the reactivity is unsmoothed strobing or if the splat reveals holes where the performer is.

steps.title: Cut the 60-second piece
steps.goal: Edit a vertical cut intercutting real performance and the reacting splat.
steps.prompt:
Assemble a 60-second vertical (9:16) edit. Intercut real performance footage, honest and documentary in the Lomax spirit, with the reacting splat. The place itself should move with the tune.
Sync the cut to the processed room audio.
Open on something that establishes the real place, so the splat reads as that same room transformed, not a generic effect. Follow the @honeycrush.online proof that a two-person, one-camera shoot can carry a strong mood.
Keep the musicians and the place named in the caption. No generated faces, no synthetic performance.
Export at the platform's preferred vertical resolution and frame rate. Keep the project file and a frame-accurate marker list so re-exports match. Export a square or landscape version too if the act wants it for other platforms, from the same timeline.
steps.expect: edit/final_60s.mp4, a vertical cut synced to the room audio, with an honest caption naming the place and players.
steps.audit: Confirm the edit opens on the real place and that the viewer can tell the splat is that room. Confirm the audio is the convolved room take, not the dry take. Fail if the piece hides the real performance behind effects, or runs long enough to lose a short-form viewer.

steps.title: A/B against a plain performance video
steps.goal: Test whether the splat format earns its complexity with the audience.
steps.prompt:
Make a control: a plain performance video of the same tune in the same room, same length, no splat.
Post the splat cut and the control on the same account, matched for day and time of day, far enough apart not to cannibalize each other, and ideally counterbalanced across two tunes.
Pre-register the metric: average watch-through (percent of the video watched) and completion rate.
Collect the platform analytics for both after a set window (for example 7 days).
State the pass rule in advance: the splat cut holds watch-through at least as well as the plain video. If it loses watch-through, the format is decoration, per the dive's falsifier. Record the view count, likes and shares alongside retention, but judge on retention, since reach depends on the algorithm. Keep the raw analytics screenshots in ab_test/ as evidence for the audit.
steps.expect: ab_test/ with the control video, the posting log, and a metrics sheet of watch-through and completion for both.
steps.audit: Confirm the two posts are matched for time and length, or the comparison is confounded. If total views are too low to distinguish the two, extend the window rather than calling a result. Fail if the metric was chosen after seeing the numbers.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Judge the piece by capture quality, acoustic match and audience retention.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) The .splat opens and reacts in a desktop browser with no holes in the performance area.
(b) The processed RT60 is within 10% of the room's measured RT60.
(c) A blind listening test: people match the processed audio to the room better than chance.
(d) The A/B watch-through and completion of the splat cut versus the control.
(e) The falsifier: are interior scans too noisy to read, or does the splat cut lose watch-through? If either, say the format is a gimmick for this room.
Write report.md with the sections Capture, Acoustics, Render, Edit, A/B Result, Falsifier and Gaps. State plainly whether the format earned its complexity. Rank the gaps by effect on the result.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a ranked gap list.
steps.audit: Any acoustic 'match' without the RT60 numbers is downgraded to unverified. Any A/B 'win' without matched posts is downgraded to inconclusive. Confirm the report names the real place and musicians. Fail if the falsifier section is missing.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are an independent reviewer: a recording engineer plus a volumetric artist. Open report.md, capture/, audio/, render/, edit/ and ab_test/.
1. Enumerate every claim: scan quality, the acoustic match, the reactivity, and the A/B result. Mark each verified, unverified or false.
2. Open the .splat yourself and look for holes in the performance area. Load it in Gausseous and confirm it reacts.
3. Recompute the processed take's RT60 and compare it with the measured room RT60. Is it within 10%?
4. Confirm the audio in the final edit is the convolved room take, not the dry take or a preset reverb.
5. Check the A/B: are the posts matched for time and length, and was the metric pre-registered?
6. List what is missing: scan holes, a clap-not-sweep IR, no dry take, an underpowered A/B.
7. Rank the gaps by effect on the result. Fix the top three now where possible (re-balance the wet/dry, raise the reactivity gates). Report what needs a reshoot and why.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps' and an A-F grade on whether the format earned its complexity.
self_questions: Does the splat have holes or noise where the performer stands?
Was the impulse response a proper sine sweep, or just a clap I am overselling?
Is the dry take actually dry, or is the room already baked into it?
Is the processed RT60 within 10% of the measured room RT60?
Does the audio-reactivity read as musical, or is it twitchy strobing?
Did I use the convolved room audio in the final edit, not the dry take?
Does the edit establish the real place before showing the splat?
Are the A/B posts matched for time of day and length?
Did I pre-register the watch-through metric before seeing the numbers?
Does the splat cut hold the viewer as long as the plain performance video?
Did I name the place and musicians honestly, with no synthetic performance?
validation_oracles: The exported .splat opens and reacts in Gausseous in a desktop browser at an acceptable frame rate, with no holes in the performance area.
Acoustic match: the processed take's RT60 is within about 10% of the room's measured RT60 from the impulse response.
Blind listening test: people match the processed audio to the correct room better than chance.
A/B retention: watch-through and completion of the splat cut versus a matched plain-performance control on the same account.
The pre-registered falsifier: interior scans too noisy to read, or the splat cut losing watch-through, means the format is a gimmick for this room.
failure_modes: Noisy low-light scan. Tell: holes and floaters where the performer stands. Fix: rescan with even light and overlapping coverage, or fall back to DIY LiDAR for big dark rooms.
Fake room sound. Tell: a reverb preset instead of the measured IR. Fix: deconvolve a real sweep and match RT60 within 10%.
Baked-in room on the source. Tell: no dry take, so the IR adds reverb on top of reverb. Fix: always capture a dry close-mic or DI take.
Twitchy reactivity. Tell: the splat strobes on transients unrelated to the music. Fix: gate and smooth each band, and tune on sustained drones.
Effect over substance. Tell: the real place and performance vanish behind filters. Fix: open on the room and keep the documentary core.
Confounded A/B. Tell: the two posts went out at different times or lengths. Fix: match posting time and length and pre-register the metric.
agent_direction: Capture is the bottleneck, so get the room right in one session: a clean splat, a proper sine-sweep IR, and a dry take. A bad scan cannot be fixed later. Cache the .splat, the IR and the dry take under capture/ and never overwrite the originals. Do the deconvolution and convolution in the main thread, since the RT60 match gates everything downstream. Spawn a sub-agent for the Gausseous reactivity tuning, giving it the processed audio and the per-band mapping goals. Do not post to the act's public account, and do not publish anyone's likeness, without explicit permission. Ask the human for the room, the permission to scan it, and the performance footage at the start. Return capture/, audio/, render/, edit/, ab_test/, report.md and audit.md. The final message states the RT60 match, whether the splat reacts cleanly, and the A/B watch-through verdict.

one_shot:
ROLE
You are a design-systems lead who treats a distinctive voice as a measurable, ownable asset, not a prompt trick.

CONTEXT
The saved posts show the problem and the escape.
- @adam_ha_yes and @nateherkai: the standard stack everyone feeds their agent, 21st.dev, getdesign.md, Impeccable, awesome-design-md, a 'taste' skill, Figma MCP and Playwright. When everyone uses it, the output converges.
- @designteamofone: 'we've lost the plot on the exploratory nature of design.'
- @itsdesignertom: AI gets 80% there, the human finishes the 20%.
- @rndyrbrts: turn taste into data and back. Manifest, measure 'palette, contrast, density, spacing, motion', 'tag behavior, not adjectives', cluster into visual DNA channels, generate from the rules.
- @6ab3 archives: the Internet Archive rave-zine and arcade-flyer collections, and the David Rumsey map collection, 150,000+ historical maps.
- @rajistics: the TensorBoard Embedding Projector, where 'cold' pulls in 'Soviet' and 'war'.
- @chase.variantai: parameterized JSON image-prompt profiles.
- @therobertta: StopSlop removes AI tells but 'the missing opinion survives the edit' - deleting tells is not having a position.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- License first. Verify every image is public domain or permissively licensed, item by item. 'On archive.org' is not a license. Drop anything unverified, and record the license per item.
- Scrape politely: respect robots.txt, rate-limit, and cache.
- Rules from evidence, behavior tags not adjectives. No 'futuristic'; yes 'dense grid, high-contrast, hand-cut edges'.
- Prove the clusters are real before building on them.
- Prove the result is distinguishable from the stock stack, or admit the corpus added nothing.

DELIVERABLES
1. corpus/: a scraper, manifest.csv (url, local file, resolution, license, source collection) for 2,000 to 5,000 images, deduplicated by perceptual hash.
2. embed/: open_clip embeddings, a UMAP projection, HDBSCAN clusters, and stability.md reporting the adjusted Rand index across min_cluster_size and seeds, plus an Embedding Projector export.
3. design/: for 3 to 5 chosen clusters, a DESIGN.md each (palette as tokens, type scale, grid, texture, motion) and a parameterized JSON image-prompt profile.
4. pages/: the same landing page built three ways, stock toolkit, cluster A and cluster B, with Playwright screenshots in light and dark.
5. blind_test/: the rater protocol, the responses, and a chi-square or exact test against chance.
6. report.md.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List the images dropped for unverifiable license, clusters that dissolve under re-clustering, DESIGN.md rules not actually reflected in the pages, and a blind test with too few raters. Fill what you can. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Is every image actually clear to use? Are my clusters real structure or embedding noise? Do my tags describe behavior or mood? Can anyone actually tell my pages from the stock page?

Also note: @rndyrbrts' own room-color probe and taste-to-data pipeline is the embryonic version of this - he extracts behavior from a moodboard and generates from the rules. You are doing the same thing but with an owned public-domain corpus and a falsifiable distinctiveness test, so the voice is defensible rather than just personal.

STOP
Stop when the clusters are stable, the three pages are built and screenshotted, and the blind test has run. Stop and ask before training any image model on the corpus.

RETURN
Return corpus/, embed/, design/, pages/, blind_test/ and report.md with the sections Corpus, Clusters, Design Rules, Pages, Blind Test and Gaps.

steps.title: Scrape one archive and verify its license
steps.goal: Build a license-clean corpus of 2,000 to 5,000 images from one archive.
steps.prompt:
Pick one archive: the Internet Archive rave-zine collection (archive.org/details/ravezines), the arcade-flyer collection (archive.org/details/arcadeflyers), or the David Rumsey map collection (archive.org/details/david-rumsey-map-collection).
Use the Internet Archive's API or metadata endpoints, respect robots.txt, rate-limit requests, and cache raw responses.
For every item, capture its license or rights statement from the item metadata. Keep only items that are public domain or carry a permissive license. 'Hosted on archive.org' is not a license, so drop anything whose rights are unclear.
Download 2,000 to 5,000 images at usable resolution. Deduplicate by perceptual hash.
Write manifest.csv: url, local file, resolution, license, rights source, source collection. Record the archive collection's total size so you can state what fraction you sampled, since a biased sample skews the clusters. Keep a fetch-date column, because archive items and their rights statements can change.
steps.expect: corpus/ with the scraper, cached metadata, downloaded images, and manifest.csv of 2,000 to 5,000 deduplicated, license-verified rows.
steps.audit: Sample 30 rows and manually confirm each license against the live item page. If more than 10% are mislabeled, fix the license logic and rescrape. Confirm robots.txt was respected and requests were rate-limited. Fail if any image has an empty or unverified license field.

steps.title: Embed, cluster and prove the clusters are real
steps.goal: Turn the corpus into embeddings and clusters that survive re-running.
steps.prompt:
Embed every image with open_clip (ViT-B-32 or ViT-L-14). Save the vectors.
Reduce with UMAP for visualization, and cluster the full-dimensional embeddings with HDBSCAN.
Prove the clusters are structure, not noise: re-run HDBSCAN across min_cluster_size values (for example 15, 30, 60) and across 3 random seeds for UMAP. Compute the adjusted Rand index between runs. Keep only clusters that persist with a high ARI.
Export the embeddings and labels to the TensorBoard Embedding Projector and inspect neighborhoods by eye, the way @rajistics inspects word2vec.
Name the stable clusters by what they visually are, deferring the behavior tags to step 3. Store the reduced 2D coordinates so the Projector view is reproducible. Note how many images land in the HDBSCAN noise bucket, because a large noise fraction means the corpus has no strong structure and the whole thesis is weak.
steps.expect: embed/ with vectors, a UMAP plot, cluster labels, stability.md with ARI across settings, and a Projector export.
steps.audit: If the adjusted Rand index between runs is low (clusters reshuffle), the structure is weak, so report that and keep only clusters above your ARI threshold. Confirm the Projector export loads. Fail if clusters are claimed stable without the ARI numbers.

steps.title: Write DESIGN.md and JSON profiles from evidence
steps.goal: Convert 3 to 5 chosen clusters into reusable design rules and prompt profiles.
steps.prompt:
For each of the 3 to 5 clusters you want to keep, measure the visual behavior across its images: palette (k-means in Lab, as tokens), contrast, edge and element density, whitespace, dominant type characteristics, grid tendency, texture and any motion cues.
Write a DESIGN.md per cluster in the awesome-design-md style, but derived from your corpus, not borrowed. Use behavior tags, not adjectives: 'dense grid, hand-cut edges, high-contrast duotone', never 'retro-cool'.
Write a parameterized JSON image-prompt profile per cluster, in @chase.variantai's format, with the swappable values (palette, density, texture, subject) exposed.
State, per cluster, what the system should always do and never do, the @rndyrbrts constraint.
Keep every rule traceable to measured features of the cluster.
steps.expect: design/ with 3 to 5 DESIGN.md files and matching JSON profiles, each with palette tokens and behavior tags.
steps.audit: Spot-check that each rule traces to a measured feature, not an impression. Grep the DESIGN.md files for banned adjective-only tags and replace them. Fail if a palette is hand-picked rather than extracted, or if any DESIGN.md has no always/never constraints.

steps.title: Build the same page three ways
steps.goal: Produce the stock-toolkit control and two archive-anchored variants for comparison.
steps.prompt:
Define one landing page brief: the same copy, sections and content for all three builds.
Build it three ways with the agent:
- Control: the stock stack (Impeccable plus awesome-design-md plus 21st.dev components), the @adam_ha_yes and @nateherkai setup.
- Variant A: driven only by cluster A's DESIGN.md and JSON profile.
- Variant B: driven only by cluster B's DESIGN.md and JSON profile.
Keep the content identical so only the design voice differs.
Screenshot all three with Playwright at desktop and mobile widths, in light and dark.
This is the @itsdesignertom 80/20 test made concrete: does the corpus-derived 20% actually change the result? Keep a shared components and copy file that all three builds import, so identical content is enforced mechanically, not by hand. Record which stock-stack skills the control used, for the audit.
steps.expect: pages/ with three built pages sharing content, and Playwright screenshots at two widths and two themes.
steps.audit: Confirm the three pages use the same copy and sections, so the only variable is the design voice. If the control secretly borrowed from the clusters, rebuild it clean. Fail if the screenshots are missing a width or theme, or if the content differs across builds.

steps.title: Blind rater test against the stock page
steps.goal: Measure whether the archive-anchored pages are distinguishable from the stock output.
steps.prompt:
Design a blind test. Show 15 or more raters outside your team the three pages (control, A, B) without labels, in randomized order.
Ask each rater: group these by visual voice; which feels most distinctive; and which two look most alike. Also ask them to guess which one is the 'generic AI' design.
Score it: can raters separate the archive-anchored pages from the stock page better than chance? Use a chi-square or an exact test and report the p-value and effect size.
This is the dive's falsifier, stated up front: if raters cannot tell the archive pages from the stock page better than chance, the corpus added nothing the shared stack lacks.
Also run @therobertta's StopSlop check in reverse: does each page take a visual position, or just avoid tells?
steps.expect: blind_test/ with the protocol, randomized stimuli, rater responses, and a statistical test with a p-value.
steps.audit: Confirm the raters are outside the team and saw no labels. If fewer than 15 raters responded, mark the result underpowered rather than conclusive. Fail if the distinguishing metric was chosen after seeing responses.

steps.title: Regurgitation and license safety check
steps.goal: Make sure the outputs are original and the whole pipeline is license-clean.
steps.prompt:
Check that nothing in the generated pages or any generated imagery is a near-copy of a source image. Compute perceptual-hash (phash) distances between every output asset and the corpus. Flag any distance below a set threshold (for example 8) as a potential copy and remove or regenerate it.
Re-verify the license trail end to end: every corpus image used in training or generation inputs has a recorded public-domain or permissive license, and that license permits derivative and commercial use.
If you intend to train a small image model or LoRA on a cluster for hero imagery, stop here and get explicit human approval first, and document the training-data license basis.
Write a one-page rights summary a lawyer could read.
steps.expect: a phash report of outputs versus corpus, a license re-verification, and rights_summary.md.
steps.audit: Any output within the phash threshold of a source is pulled before shipping. Confirm the rights summary cites the archive's actual license terms, not an assumption. Fail if any training step ran without recorded license basis or human approval.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Deliver the distinctiveness verdict, the falsifier result and the gaps.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) Blind raters distinguish the archive pages from the stock page better than chance (p-value and effect size).
(b) Cluster stability: kept clusters persist across settings by adjusted Rand index.
(c) Regurgitation: no output within the phash threshold of a source.
(d) License audit: every used image verified public domain or permissive.
(e) The falsifier: if raters cannot tell the pages apart, say plainly the corpus added nothing and the shared stack would have done.
Write report.md with the sections Corpus, Clusters, Design Rules, Pages, Blind Test, Rights, Falsifier and Gaps. State whether the corpus produced a defensible, distinguishable voice. Rank the gaps by impact on that claim.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a ranked gap list.
steps.audit: Any distinctiveness claim without the blind-test p-value is downgraded to unverified. Any cluster used without a stability score is flagged. Confirm the rights section covers every used image. Fail if the falsifier section is missing.

2. Sample 20 corpus rows and confirm the license against the live item pages.
3. Recompute cluster stability: re-run HDBSCAN with a different min_cluster_size and compare the adjusted Rand index against stability.md.
4. Check the three pages use identical content, so the comparison is clean.
5. Recompute the blind-test statistic from the raw responses. Does the p-value support the distinctiveness claim? Are there 15 or more outside raters?
6. Run phash between the output assets and the corpus and list any near-copies.
7. List what is missing: dropped-license images, dissolving clusters, rules not reflected in the pages, an underpowered blind test.
8. Rank the gaps by impact. Fix the top three now. Report what you could not fix and why.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps' and an A-F grade on whether the voice is defensible.

Do my clusters survive re-running with different parameters, or do they reshuffle?
Do my tags describe visual behavior, or did adjectives like 'moody' slip back in?
Does each DESIGN.md rule trace to a measured feature of its cluster?
Did the stock control secretly borrow from my clusters, confounding the test?
Is the page content truly identical across the three builds?
Can outside raters tell the archive pages from the stock page better than chance?
Does each archive page take a visual position, or just avoid AI tells, per the StopSlop lesson?
Is any generated asset a near-copy of a source image by perceptual hash?

If the falsifier fired, am I willing to say the corpus added nothing?
validation_oracles: Blind raters (15 or more, outside the team) distinguish the archive-anchored pages from the stock-toolkit page better than chance, by a chi-square or exact test with a reported p-value.
Cluster stability: the kept clusters persist across min_cluster_size values and UMAP seeds, measured by adjusted Rand index.
Regurgitation check: no generated asset falls within the perceptual-hash threshold of any source image.
License audit: every used image is verified public domain or permissively licensed against its live item page.
A practitioner design review confirms the pages actually follow their cluster's DESIGN.md rules.
failure_modes: License assumption. Tell: images used because they were 'on archive.org'. Fix: verify rights per item and drop the unverifiable.
Noise clusters. Tell: clusters reshuffle on re-run, low adjusted Rand index. Fix: keep only stable clusters and report the ARI.
Adjective tags. Tell: DESIGN.md says 'futuristic' with no measured basis. Fix: behavior tags traced to extracted features.
Confounded control. Tell: the stock page quietly used cluster colors. Fix: build the control from the stock stack alone, with identical content.
Unfalsifiable claim. Tell: 'it looks more distinctive' with no blind test. Fix: run the rater test and report the p-value, and accept the falsifier.

Spawn one sub-agent for the embedding and clustering job (step 2), which is compute-heavy and isolated, and give it the manifest and the stability protocol. Keep the DESIGN.md authoring and the blind-test design in the main thread, since they need judgment. Do not train any image model or LoRA on the corpus without explicit human approval and a documented license basis: stop and ask. Do not ship any asset that is a near-copy of a source image. Ask the human at the start which archive to mine and who can serve as blind raters. Return corpus/, embed/, design/, pages/, blind_test/, report.md and audit.md. mission: Build a local, fully offline melody-genealogy engine that does by machine what Chance McCoy does by ear: cluster public-domain recordings into tune families and map how melodies travelled across centuries and languages. The pieces are a license-verified corpus of 200 to 500 public-domain recordings, pitch-contour and audio embeddings in ChromaDB in the SentrySearch layout, a lineage graph with timestamped links to sources, and one cleared sample pack with a provenance sheet. Done means known variant families cluster above chance (the falsifier), every recording's rights are checked recording-by-recording, and the lineage claims are backed by sources, not vibes.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: An ethnomusicologist and a music-information-retrieval engineer would not trust a single embedding space to declare two tunes related. They would extract an explicit, transposition-invariant melodic representation (a pitch-contour or interval sequence), test the clustering against a labelled ground-truth set of known tune families from the folk-song literature, and report precision and recall, not a pretty graph. They would treat the Platonic Representation idea as a hypothesis to test, not a license to assume cross-source similarity is meaningful. And they would be ruthless about rights: a 1929 composition can be public domain while a specific 1929 recording's rights differ, so they would verify composition and recording separately before calling anything a 'cleared sample'.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Public-domain recordings: Library of Congress collections (the Lomax field recordings, @dimestoreradio's Nimrod Workman lineage), Internet Archive 78-rpm collections, and the Prelinger ephemeral films with period audio. The specific anchors Chance McCoy names: Doc Watson's 'Shady Grove' in D-Dorian traced to Jean Ritchie and Child Ballad #81 'Matty Groves', and 'Sally in the Garden' from Crockett's Kentucky Mountaineers' 1929 Brunswick 291, related to the Ozark 'Hog-Eye Man' tunes. Cross-language edges: ABBA's 'The Winner Takes It All' in Mandarin, Ievan Polkka in Russian. The SentrySearch repo (ssrajadh/sentrysearch) as the local-search layout. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis paper.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: A melody extractor for monophonic pitch contours (CREPE or pYIN via librosa), quantized to interval sequences for transposition invariance. An open audio embedding model (such as a CLAP audio encoder) for timbral similarity. ChromaDB for local vector storage, following SentrySearch's fully-offline layout. HDBSCAN or agglomerative clustering on both representations. A labelled ground-truth set of known tune families (Child ballad numbers, Roud folk-song index entries) to score against. NetworkX plus a force-directed web view for the lineage graph, with timestamped links back to each source recording. Precision/recall and adjusted Rand index against ground truth.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: Known variant families clustering together above chance: do 'Shady Grove' and 'Matty Groves' land near each other, and do the 'Hog-Eye Man' tunes group? Scored by precision, recall and adjusted Rand index against a labelled set from the Child and Roud indices (the dive's falsifier). A rights audit clearing composition and recording separately for every sample in the pack. Producer pickup of the released free sample pack, measured. A cross-check that the Mandarin and Russian re-lyricised versions sit on the correct melody edges despite different words.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt:

2. Extract transposition-invariant pitch contours (CREPE or pYIN, quantized to intervals) and audio embeddings (a CLAP encoder). Store both in ChromaDB in the SentrySearch offline layout.
3. Cluster both representations. Score them against a labelled ground-truth set of known families from the Child and Roud indices, including 'Shady Grove' / 'Matty Groves' (Child #81) and the 'Hog-Eye Man' tunes. Report precision, recall and adjusted Rand index.
4. Only if families cluster above chance, build a lineage graph in NetworkX with timestamped links to each source recording.
5. Package one cluster as a public-domain sample pack with a per-sample provenance sheet clearing composition and recording.
6. Pre-register the falsifier: if known families do not cluster above chance, the hand method stays the only method.
Return the corpus manifest, embeddings, cluster scores, the lineage graph, and the cleared sample pack.

- @ssrajadh/sentrysearch: a 100% local video-search engine, type a query and it returns timestamps, using Qwen3-VL embeddings and ChromaDB. The layout to copy for audio.
- @lizthedeveloper: the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, shared embedding spaces across models, framed as 'AI telepathy'. A hypothesis to test, not assume.
- @baauer: Passion Pit's 'Sleepyhead' sampled Mary O'Hara's 1958 'Oro Mo Bhaidin'. @aklmadz: where producers hunt samples.
- @lilithsomething and @kvashenaya: 'The Winner Takes It All' in Mandarin and Ievan Polkka in Russian, melody kept, lyrics re-written, lineage edges.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Rights, recording by recording. A public-domain composition does not make a given recording public domain. Verify composition and recording separately, and drop anything not clearly cleared.
- Fully local, like SentrySearch. No recording leaves the machine.
- Transposition-invariant melody: compare interval sequences, not raw pitch.
- Prove families cluster above chance before building any lineage graph.
- Every lineage edge links to a timestamped source recording. No uncited edges.

DELIVERABLES
1. corpus/: a fetcher and manifest.csv (source, url, year, composition rights, recording rights, cleared y/n) for 200 to 500 public-domain recordings.
2. index/: pitch contours (CREPE or pYIN, quantized to intervals) and CLAP audio embeddings, both in ChromaDB in the SentrySearch offline layout.
3. eval/: a labelled ground-truth set of known families from the Child and Roud indices, and a score of the clustering by precision, recall and adjusted Rand index.
4. lineage/: a NetworkX graph and a force-directed web view, each edge carrying a timestamped link to its source recording, built only if the eval passes.
5. pack/: one cluster as a sample pack with a per-sample provenance sheet clearing composition and recording.
6. report.md.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
List recordings dropped for unclear rights, families with no ground-truth label, edges with no timestamped source, and clusters that do not beat chance. Fill what you can. Mark the rest UNFILLED.

SELF-QUESTIONS
Is each recording's rights cleared, not just the composition's? Do 'Shady Grove' and 'Matty Groves' actually cluster together? Is my melody representation transposition-invariant? Does every lineage edge cite a source?

STOP
Stop when the clustering is scored against ground truth and, if it passes, the lineage graph and one cleared pack are built. Stop and report the falsifier if families do not beat chance.

RETURN
Return corpus/, index/, eval/, lineage/, pack/ and report.md with the sections Corpus, Index, Evaluation, Lineage, Sample Pack and Gaps.

steps.title: Gather recordings and clear rights twice
steps.goal: Build a 200 to 500 recording corpus where composition and recording rights are each verified.
steps.prompt:
Pull 200 to 500 recordings from public-domain sources: Library of Congress collections (including the Lomax field recordings and the Nimrod Workman lineage @dimestoreradio shows), Internet Archive 78-rpm collections, and Prelinger film audio. Include the anchors @chancemccoymusic names: 'Shady Grove' versions (Doc Watson, Jean Ritchie), 'Matty Groves', 'Sally in the Garden' (Crockett's Kentucky Mountaineers, Brunswick 291), and 'Hog-Eye Man' tunes.
For each recording, verify rights twice: the composition (often public domain if pre-1929 in the US) and the specific recording (a 1929 recording's rights can differ). Record both in manifest.csv with the rights source, and set cleared=y only when both are clear.
Fetch locally and keep audio on the machine. Record the duration and recording year of each item, since the lineage graph orients edges by date. Keep a cleared-count so you know how many recordings are actually usable in the sample pack, separate from the full corpus.
steps.expect: corpus/ with the audio, and manifest.csv of 200 to 500 rows carrying composition rights, recording rights, year, source URL and a cleared flag.
steps.audit: Sample 20 rows and confirm both the composition and the recording rights against the source. If a recording's rights are unclear, set cleared=n and exclude it from the sample pack. Fail if any row conflates composition rights with recording rights, or has an empty rights source.

steps.title: Extract transposition-invariant melody and audio embeddings
steps.goal: Represent each recording as both an interval contour and an audio embedding, stored locally.
steps.prompt:
For each recording, extract the monophonic melody with CREPE or pYIN (via librosa). Convert the pitch track to a sequence of intervals (semitone steps between successive notes) so the representation is transposition-invariant, which matters because the same tune appears in different keys and modal tunings, like the D-Dorian 'Shady Grove'.
Separately, compute an audio embedding with an open CLAP audio encoder for timbral and overall similarity.
Store both representations in ChromaDB, following the SentrySearch (ssrajadh/sentrysearch) fully-local layout: one collection for melody-interval vectors, one for audio embeddings, with metadata linking back to the recording and timestamp.
Keep everything offline.
Handle polyphonic or noisy 78s by flagging low-confidence melody extractions rather than trusting them. Store the raw pitch track alongside the quantized intervals for debugging, but index only the intervals. Note the sample rate and any resampling, since 78-rpm transfers vary and pitch extraction is sensitive to speed errors.
steps.expect: index/ with a ChromaDB store holding interval-contour and CLAP vectors per recording, plus a confidence flag on each melody extraction.
steps.audit: Verify transposition invariance: transpose a test recording by 3 semitones, re-extract, and confirm its interval sequence is nearly unchanged. If it changes a lot, fix the interval quantization. Flag melody extractions below a confidence threshold. Fail if raw pitch (not intervals) was stored.

steps.title: Build ground truth and score the clustering
steps.goal: Test whether known tune families actually cluster, before drawing any tree.
steps.prompt:
Build a labelled ground-truth set: assign known family labels from the Child ballad numbers and the Roud Folk Song Index to the recordings where the literature establishes them. At minimum: 'Shady Grove' and 'Matty Groves' as Child #81, the 'Hog-Eye Man' group, and a few unrelated control tunes that should not cluster together.
Cluster both representations (interval contours and audio embeddings) with HDBSCAN or agglomerative clustering.
Score the clustering against the ground truth: precision, recall, and adjusted Rand index. Specifically check: do 'Shady Grove' and 'Matty Groves' land in the same cluster? Do the controls stay apart?
State the falsifier up front: if known families do not cluster above chance, the embedding search is noise and the hand method stays the only method.
steps.expect: eval/ with the ground-truth labels, cluster assignments, and a score table (precision, recall, adjusted Rand index) with the known-family checks.
steps.audit: Compare against a random-label baseline to define 'above chance'. If the interval and audio representations disagree, report both and do not cherry-pick the flattering one. Fail if the Shady Grove / Matty Groves check is not explicitly reported, pass or fail.

steps.title: Build the lineage graph with cited edges
steps.goal: Map the tune family tree, but only if the evaluation passed.
steps.prompt:
Proceed only if step 3 showed known families clustering above chance. If it did not, skip to the report and record the falsifier result.
Build a lineage graph in NetworkX. Nodes are recordings or tune variants. Edges connect variants that are melodically close (by interval-contour distance), with the edge weight being the similarity.
Every edge must carry a timestamped link back to the source recording that supports it, in the SentrySearch spirit of returning exact timestamps.
Orient edges by date where the recording year is known, so the graph reads as travel over time: Renaissance ballad to Appalachian standard, 1929 Brunswick to later field recordings.
Add the cross-language edges as test cases: the Mandarin 'Winner Takes It All' and Russian Ievan Polkka should connect to their source melodies despite different lyrics.
Render a force-directed web view.
steps.expect: lineage/ with the NetworkX graph (GraphML or JSON) and an interactive force-graph view, every edge citing a timestamped source.
steps.audit: Pick 10 edges at random and confirm each links to a real source recording and timestamp. Confirm the Mandarin and Russian versions attach to the correct melody, not to each other by language. Fail if any edge has no source citation, or if the graph was built despite a failed eval.

steps.title: Package one cleared sample pack
steps.goal: Turn one validated cluster into a legally clean sample pack with provenance.
steps.prompt:
Pick one cluster that clustered cleanly and whose recordings are all cleared=y in both composition and recording rights.
Cut usable sample segments (loops, one-shots, vocal phrases) from those recordings.
Write a provenance sheet per sample: the source recording, its year, the composition and recording rights basis, and the lineage position (which tune family, which known relatives). This is the opposite of crate-digging into a clearance fight, as @baauer's 'Sleepyhead' sample story warns.
Assemble the pack with the samples, the provenance sheet, and a short written family history.
Prepare a free release and define how you will measure producer pickup (downloads, uses, tags). Keep the exact in and out points for each sample so cuts are reproducible. Note the tempo and key of each sample, because producers filter on those and it makes the pack more useful.
steps.expect: pack/ with sample files, a per-sample provenance sheet, a family-history note, and a pickup-measurement plan.
steps.audit: Confirm every sample in the pack traces to a cleared=y recording, with both rights cleared. If any sample's recording rights are unclear, pull it. Fail if the pack ships without a provenance sheet, or includes a recording cleared only at the composition level.

steps.title: Test the Platonic Representation claim
steps.goal: Check whether cross-source embedding similarity is real signal, honestly.
steps.prompt:
The dive leans on @lizthedeveloper's framing of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: different models' embedding spaces converge, so melodic similarity might be findable across sources. Test it rather than assume it.
Take the interval-contour similarity and the CLAP audio similarity for the same pairs of recordings. Correlate them. If two independent representations agree on which tunes are related, that is evidence the similarity is real structure, not an artifact of one model.
Report the correlation and where the two disagree, since disagreements are the interesting cases: same melody, different timbre (a cross-language cover), or similar timbre, different melody (a false friend).
Do not overclaim: a positive correlation supports the method, it does not prove any specific lineage edge.
steps.expect: a correlation analysis between the melodic and audio similarity spaces, with the agreement and disagreement cases listed.
steps.audit: If the two representations correlate weakly, say so plainly and lean on the interval contours (the musically meaningful one) for lineage, not the audio embedding. Fail if a lineage edge rests only on audio-timbre similarity with no melodic support.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Deliver the clustering verdict, the falsifier result and the ranked gaps.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracle pass:
(a) Known families cluster above chance: the precision, recall and adjusted Rand index against the Child/Roud ground truth, and the explicit 'Shady Grove' / 'Matty Groves' check.
(b) Transposition invariance of the melody representation, verified by the transpose test.
(c) Every lineage edge cites a timestamped source recording.
(d) Every sample in the pack is cleared at both the composition and recording level.
(e) The falsifier: if known families do not beat chance, say plainly the embedding search is noise and the hand method stays the only method.
Write report.md with the sections Corpus, Index, Evaluation, Lineage, Sample Pack, Platonic-Representation Check and Gaps. State whether the engine actually finds tune families. Rank the gaps by impact.
steps.expect: report.md, a five-row oracle table, and a ranked gap list.
steps.audit: Any lineage claim without a cited source is removed. Any 'above chance' claim without the random baseline is downgraded. Confirm the pack's rights are cleared at both levels. Fail if the falsifier section is missing or the Shady Grove check is absent.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are an independent reviewer: an ethnomusicologist plus an ML engineer. Open report.md, corpus/manifest.csv, index/, eval/, lineage/ and pack/.
1. Enumerate every claim: corpus rights, clustering scores, specific lineage edges, and sample clearances. Mark each verified, unverified or false.
2. Sample 20 corpus rows and confirm composition and recording rights are each verified, not conflated.
3. Recompute the clustering scores against the ground truth, including the Shady Grove / Matty Groves check and the controls. Is it above a random-label baseline?
4. Run the transpose test on a recording and confirm the interval contour is stable.
5. Pick 10 lineage edges and confirm each cites a real timestamped source. Confirm cross-language covers attach to the correct melody.
6. Confirm every sample in the pack is cleared at both the composition and recording level.
7. List what is missing: unclear-rights recordings, families with no label, uncited edges, clusters that do not beat chance.
8. Rank the gaps by impact. Fix the top three now. Report what you could not fix and why.
Return audit.md with the columns claim, status, evidence and fix, plus 'Remaining gaps' and an A-F grade on whether the engine finds real tune families.
self_questions: Is each recording cleared at both the composition and recording level, not just one?
Do 'Shady Grove' and 'Matty Groves' actually land in the same cluster?
Is my melody representation transposition-invariant, so different keys and modal tunings match?
Does the clustering beat a random-label baseline, or am I seeing patterns in noise?
Does every lineage edge cite a timestamped source recording?
Do the Mandarin and Russian re-lyricised versions attach to the right melody despite different words?
Do the interval-contour and audio-embedding spaces agree, and what do their disagreements mean?
Am I resting any lineage edge on timbre similarity alone, with no melodic support?
Did noisy 78 transfers produce low-confidence melody extractions I am over-trusting?
Is every sample in the pack from a cleared=y recording?
If the falsifier fired, am I willing to say the hand method stays the only method?
validation_oracles: Known tune families cluster above chance against a labelled Child/Roud ground-truth set, scored by precision, recall and adjusted Rand index, with the 'Shady Grove' / 'Matty Groves' (Child #81) check reported explicitly.
Transposition invariance: transposing a recording and re-extracting leaves its interval contour nearly unchanged.
Every lineage edge links to a timestamped source recording, SentrySearch-style, with no uncited edges.
Every sample in the released pack is cleared separately at the composition and recording level, with a provenance sheet.
Agreement between the interval-contour and CLAP audio similarity spaces supports that found similarities are real structure, not one model's artifact.
failure_modes: Rights conflation. Tell: a 1929 recording called public domain because the tune is old. Fix: verify composition and recording separately and clear both before sampling.
Key-dependent matching. Tell: the same tune in two keys does not cluster. Fix: compare transposition-invariant interval sequences, not raw pitch.
Pattern in noise. Tell: a pretty graph with no ground-truth score. Fix: score against known families versus a random baseline before drawing the tree.
Uncited edges. Tell: the lineage graph asserts a link with no source. Fix: require a timestamped source recording on every edge or drop it.
Timbre false friends. Tell: two tracks cluster because they share a scratchy 78 sound, not a melody. Fix: lead with interval contours and treat audio embedding as secondary.
Overclaiming telepathy. Tell: the Platonic Representation idea used to assert lineage. Fix: test the correlation and claim only method support, not specific edges.
agent_direction: Rights clearance is the gate: a corpus that conflates composition and recording rights makes the sample pack a liability, so verify both before anything else. Keep all audio local, in the SentrySearch spirit, and never upload a recording. Cache the ChromaDB store and the extracted contours so re-runs are fast. Spawn one sub-agent for the melody and audio extraction over the whole corpus, since it is the heavy, parallelizable step, and give it the confidence-flagging rule. Keep the ground-truth evaluation and the lineage graph in the main thread, because they carry the verdict. Do not build the lineage graph or ship a sample pack if the clustering fails the ground-truth test: report the falsifier instead. Ask the human at the start which archives and which known families to anchor on. Return corpus/, index/, eval/, lineage/, pack/, report.md and audit.md. The final message states the clustering score, the Shady Grove / Matty Groves result, and whether the engine finds real tune families.
